Bahrain's top court upheld the conviction in 2021, with confiscation of remittances put at 184 million US dollars, 967 million euros, 53 million dirhams and 235 billion riyals. Iran scores 43 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, 27th of 194.
p:MWI: The Reserve Bank of Malawi issues the kwacha, and presidents have removed its leaders twice. President Joyce Banda removed governor Perks Ligoya, according to two unnamed sources, with Charles Chuka reportedly chosen to succeed him and no official reason given; the date is not stated. Newly elected president Lazarus Chakwera dismissed governor Dalitso Kabambe and appointed Wilson Banda on 8 July 2020. After a forensic audit of the bank's payments between January 2019 and June 2020, the state charged Kabambe and three others with abuse of office, negligence, money laundering and causing loss of public funds, alleging that 4.3 billion kwacha went to FDH Bank without board approval; pleas were not taken because the charges were subject to change, and nothing is proven. In December 2021 police arrested Kabambe and Joseph Mwanamvekha, saying the two procured and masterminded the falsification of gross liability and net reserve base returns to make the International Monetary Fund believe Malawi was meeting the conditions of its Extended Credit Facility loan; that too stands only as an accusation. In January 2026 President Peter Mutharika appointed Henry Mathanga deputy governor, although the bank had dismissed him after a disciplinary inquiry and he faces criminal charges, and critics say the appointment breaches section 16(2) of the Reserve Bank of Malawi Act. Its 2,000-kwacha note is printed by Giesecke & Devrient. Malawi scores 35 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:VNM: The State Bank of Vietnam issues the dong and moves its rate against the dollar in small steps rather than leaving it to the market. On paper its law gives it almost no independence, 0.301 of 1 and 154th of 155 places, and government pressure was reported in 6 of 37 quarters up to 2018. In April 2024 the Ho Chi Minh City People's Court sentenced Truong My Lan, chair of Van Thinh Phat, to death for fraud at Saigon Commercial Bank, finding that she had ordered subordinates to bribe State Bank inspectors; state media reported that head banking inspector Do Thi Nhan took 5.2 million US dollars and deputy chief inspector Nguyen Van Hung 300,000. In October 2011 Securency, a subsidiary of the Reserve Bank of Australia, pleaded guilty in the Supreme Court of Victoria to conspiring to give benefits to foreign public officials to win banknote business with Vietnam's note-issuing authority between 2001 and 2004; the officials are not named. The bank's notes are printed by the state-owned National Banknote Printing Factory, whose chairman the Governor appoints. Cao Si Kiem, governor from 1989 to 1997, joined the board of the joint-stock commercial DongA Bank in March 2012 and became its chairman on 26 April 2014. The bank is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, and Vietnam scores 33 of 100 on exposure to outside influence.
p:IRQ: The Central Bank of Iraq issues the dinar and keeps it within a band of 2 percent or less against the US dollar. It scores 36 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and 0.733 of 1 for the independence written into its law, where 1 means the bank holds the power and 0 the government. In 2012 Iraq's Board of Supreme Audit examined the bank's daily auctions of dollars to banks and found that most transactions rested on fraudulent paperwork; the country's top auditor told US officials that up to 800 million dollars a week was leaving Iraq illegally, as reported by the US Special Inspector General for Iraq Reconstruction. In October 2012 the cabinet removed governor Sinan al-Shabibi and named a successor while a parliamentary committee was examining possible manipulation of the dinar and charging that bank officials were abusing the dollar sales. A committee member said arrest warrants had been issued for 30 people, including al-Shabibi and his deputy Mudher Saleh, and the Supreme Judicial Council confirmed warrants without saying what the charges were. The integrity committee's chairman said the inquiry was "not about money, but about procedures", while a member of the finance committee called it "a political decision and not professional"; al-Shabibi's defence called the case politically motivated. No court outcome was ever found, so nothing was proven; he died on 8 January 2022, and the bank mourned him as a distinguished former governor. It holds 175.6 tonnes of gold, and the Board of Supreme Audit audits its accounts.
p:KOR: South Korea's money is the won, issued by the Bank of Korea, which scores 24 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Two cases are recorded, both ending in conviction. Between 2022 and 2023 a currency-exchange employee at the bank's Daejeon Sejong-Chungnam headquarters broke the rule that older coins leave the vault first, at a coin collector's request, letting 240,000 one-hundred-won coins from 2018 and 2019 go out ahead of 2017 coins; the collector made about 180 million won selling them and gave the employee about 55 million, and the Daejeon District Court imposed two years and six months in prison, a fine and confiscation. Between 2013 and 2015 an employee handling receipts from the bank's publication sales diverted about 56 million won to a personal account and spent about 12 million won on commemorative banknote sheets with a company card; the Seoul Central District Court gave eight months suspended for two years, the money having been repaid. Two officials came from international lenders: Hwang Geon-il of the World Bank was nominated to the rate-setting Monetary Policy Committee, and Rhee Chang-yong of the International Monetary Fund was nominated governor on 23 March 2022. Three audits cover the bank: the Board of Audit and Inspection once a year, an auditor appointed by the President on the finance minister's recommendation who serves three years and reports to the Monetary Policy Committee, and an outside accounting firm the law requires but does not name. The notes and coins are made by the state-run mint, the Korea Minting and Security Printing Corporation, the country's only maker of banknotes and coins and a close partner of the bank, and the Bank of Korea is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, whose capital has been held by central banks alone since private shares were bought back in 2001. A newspaper report of 12 February 2025 says all 104.4 tonnes of South Korea's gold, bought between 2011 and 2013, is stored at the Bank of England. That is the paper's own wording, not attributed to the Bank of Korea, so it is a claim rather than a confirmed fact.
p:VEN: The bolivar is issued by the Central Bank of Venezuela. On paper the bank is protected, scoring 0.816 of 1 on an index of 42 legal rules where 1 means the bank rather than the government holds the power, but government pressure was reported in 18 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, including 13 demands to print money. In January 2017 President Nicolas Maduro announced the firing of bank chief Nelson Merentes, who the report says handed in his resignation, and named Ricardo Sanguino to succeed him; no reason was given. In January 2020 the prosecutor Tarek William Saab said a payments head at the bank and others had forged purchase files so the bank paid about 1.7 million US dollars to three companies it had never contracted, for goods never delivered. Eight arrest warrants were sought, the case began with a complaint by the bank's president, Calixto Ortega, and no trial or conviction is reported, so the accusations are unproven. On 29 July 2022 London's High Court ruled that Venezuelan supreme court judgments backing the Maduro-appointed board should be disregarded, keeping more than 1 billion US dollars of Venezuelan gold held at the Bank of England out of Maduro's control. Russia's state printer Goznak signed a contract to print the bank's notes in November 2019. Venezuela scores 37 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:BOL: The Central Bank of Bolivia issues the boliviano, and the state audit office, the Contraloria General de la Republica, audits its accounts under the 1995 central bank law. On 17 December 2019 Guillermo Aponte took over as interim president from Pablo Ramos, who was under investigation over alleged favouring of illicit enrichment, with questions about armoured trucks said to have carried foreign currency out at unusual hours and about some 75 million US dollars in loans to state firms; that is where the matter stands, and nothing is proven. On 5 March 2021 the bank let go more than a dozen senior managers, and a former governor said the change of government had likely influenced the dismissals. On 28 April 2026 La Paz prosecutors had former president Edwin Rojas and three other former senior officials detained over seven debt-swap operations with local financial entities in June and July 2024 at inflated prices, said to have cost the state 142.3 million US dollars, with the transparency vice ministry saying price records were later altered to hide the overvaluation; the suspects deny wrongdoing, seven people are under investigation, Rojas invoked his right to silence, and it is not stated that anyone has been formally charged. About 2.62 tonnes of its gold sits in its own vaults. On 27 July 2023 it awarded its banknote tender to Oberthur Fiduciaire SAS for 25,945,787 US dollars, for 321.5 million notes of 10 to 200 bolivianos. Bolivia scores 30 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:SMR: San Marino uses the euro, and its central bank is the Central Bank of the Republic of San Marino. It scores 45 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, mainly because its money is issued or backed from abroad. The bank is owned mostly by the state: the Eccellentissima Camera della Repubblica di San Marino holds 72%, four banks hold the rest: Cassa di Risparmio della Repubblica di San Marino 16%, Banca di San Marino 6%, Banca Agricola Commerciale Istituto Bancario Sammarinese 5% and Banca Sammarinese di Investimento 1%, as of 31 December 2025. One case is recorded, from 2019 to 2020, over a 220,000 euro payment from the bank to Sandro Gozi for a consultancy that investigators suspected was fictitious. The case, against Gozi and bank president Catia Tomasetti, became public in April 2019. The Tribunal of San Marino dismissed it in 2020, finding no relevant conduct by either suspect; the article reports the consultancy was real. The bank's accounts are audited by Solution S.r.l. of Borgo Maggiore, a San Marino firm belonging to no international network, which signed its report on the 2025 accounts on 5 May 2026 and reports to the shareholders rather than to the board.
p:UKR: The National Bank of Ukraine issues the hryvnia and prints the notes itself, at the Banknote Printing and Minting Works that is part of the bank. Its independence written into law is high, 0.893 of 1, but its governors have been pushed. In January 2009 parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, voted no confidence in governor Volodymyr Stelmakh, 227 of 450 seats in favour, as the hryvnia lost nearly half its value; President Viktor Yushchenko's office called the vote illegal and kept backing him, and he was not removed. In July 2020 governor Yakiv Smolii resigned, telling President Volodymyr Zelensky that systematic political pressure had been exerted on the bank. One case is open: on 11 November 2019 the National Anti-Corruption Bureau detained seven people, including former first deputy governor Pysaruk, on suspicion of embezzling 1.2 billion hryvnia, about 49 million US dollars, from a 2014 loan the bank made to prop up VAB Bank, which was declared insolvent that November; it is unproven. Valeria Gontareva, governor from 2014 to 2017, had worked at Societe Generale, ING Bank and the Ukrainian financial services group Investment Capital Ukraine. Ukraine scores 28 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:PRY: The Central Bank of Paraguay issues the country's money, the guaraní, and scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Impeachment proceedings opened in January 2003 against President Luis González Macchi over an alleged 26 million US dollar embezzlement from the bank, and the Senate vote fell short that February. On 6 June 2006 a court in Asunción sentenced him to six years for breach of trust over 16 million US dollars diverted from Unión and Orienta, two private banks the central bank had taken over, and former banking superintendent José Pecci to eight years; an appeals court later cleared González Macchi for insufficient evidence. In February 2007 President Nicanor Duarte Frutos dismissed bank president Mónica Pérez over her disagreements with the economic team. Police searched the bank on 13 July 2021 over embezzlement and money laundering, an open investigation. On 3 November 2026 governor Carlos Carvallo resigned at President Santiago Peña's request, after a prosecutor sought an investigation around ueno, a digital lender Carvallo had headed until August 2023.
p:NOR: Norges Bank issues the Norwegian krone and is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, whose capital has been held by central banks alone since private shares were bought back in 2001. Both recorded cases come out of one hiring. On 24 March 2020 the Executive Board appointed Nicolai Tangen, who had started the hedge fund AKO Capital in 2005, to run Norges Bank Investment Management, which manages the country's oil fund. The bank's Supervisory Council warned that the hire risked breaking laws, rules and guidelines, saying Tangen still appeared to be AKO Capital's main owner with voting control, although the bank said he had cut those ties. After the Storting's finance committee raised the same concern, the Executive Board revised his terms in August 2020: he would give up his holding in AKO Capital LLP and hand it and its dividend rights to the charitable AKO Foundation, and hold his personal fund assets as bank deposits. Supervisory Board chair Julie Brodtkorb said guidelines, regulations and laws had been breached; Executive Board chair Oystein Olsen said the board had thought the existing contract was enough but accepted that the Storting took a different view. Tangen could take office on 1 September. Ernst & Young audits the bank from the 2022 financial year for six years, and at the end of 2025 103 organisations ran outside mandates worth 1,062 billion kroner. Notes were printed by Oberthur Fiduciaire in France from 2016 to 2019 and, from 2020, by Crane NXT in Malta. Norway scores 18 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:CHN: China's money, the renminbi, is issued by the People's Bank of China. The country scores 34 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and the weakest part is corruption and secrecy around the bank. Written independence scores 0.659 of 1 on an index of 42 legal rules, but the part covering the governor and the board scores only 0.04, meaning the government holds nearly all of that power; pressure from government was reported in 2 of 37 quarters surveyed between 2010 and 2018. One case is documented: in October 2024 the Huanggang Intermediate People's Court sentenced Fan Yifei, a former deputy governor, to death with a two-year reprieve, to be commuted to life without parole, for accepting property worth more than 386 million yuan through his posts at the central bank and other institutions including China Construction Bank. Its notes and coins are made by the China Banknote Printing and Minting Corporation, described as a state company inside the bank, though only Wikipedia was found saying so, and the National Audit Office audits the accounts. The governor, Pan Gongsheng, two former governors and a monetary policy committee member sit in the Group of Thirty, a private forum alongside the chief executive of Citi and a vice chairman of BlackRock. Its reach is wide: 89 swap lines, which are standing agreements to lend its currency to another central bank, 8.6 percent of world currency trading and 2,346.4 tonnes of gold.
p:AZE: The Central Bank of the Republic of Azerbaijan issues the national currency, coded AZN, held at a de facto fixed rate against the US dollar. It scores 31 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, with corruption and secrecy around it at 62. On 12 April 2022 parliament approved President Ilham Aliyev's proposal to replace governor Elman Rustamov, in post since 1995, with Taleh Kazimov, head of Pasha Bank; Rustamov became adviser to the prime minister, and no official reason and no statement from him were reported. Two cases are documented. A Vienna court found that the Austrian banknote printer OeBS had overcharged the bank by 20 per cent on banknote contracts and that the kickback went back to local decision makers; OeBS managers were convicted in 2014 and again on retrial in 2018, and no Azerbaijani official was named or tried. Austrian prosecutors also told a court that former OeBS employees had paid bribes to officials at Syrian and Azerbaijani banks for printing contracts, which stands as a prosecution allegation. In September 2009 a Baku court sentenced six former officers of the bank to between a two-year suspended sentence and eight years for abuse of power and embezzling 1.4 million AZN between 2003 and 2008. KPMG Audit Azerbaijan LLC audits the accounts, and the bank holds no gold.
p:THA: The Bank of Thailand issues the baht and prints its own notes: its history records that the Cabinet authorised it to set up the Note Printing Works in 1961, built for Thai banknote production. It is also one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, and Thailand scores 39 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. On 29 May 2001 the government fired governor Chatu Mongol Sonakul after Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said he was not satisfied with the bank's low interest rates, and Finance Minister Kittiratt Na-Ranong later pressed for governor Prasarn Trairatvorakul to be replaced over the 2.75 percent rate. More recently Pheu Thai leader Paetongtarn Shinawatra said the law keeping the bank independent gets in the way of solving economic problems, and Prime Minister Srettha Thavisin said he had no plan to remove Governor Sethaput Suthiwartnarueput. A case brought in 2001 against former governor Rerngchai Marakanond, over using the reserves to defend the baht during the Asian financial crisis, ended on 5 October 2016 when the Supreme Court upheld a ruling that he had not acted improperly, so he was acquitted. Former finance minister Surapong Suebwonglee was convicted of malfeasance for putting three representatives of banks the Bank of Thailand supervises on the committee that selects its board in 2008; he was given a one-year jail term suspended for a year and fined 20,000 baht.
p:SUR: The Central Bank of Suriname issues the Suriname dollar, which it lets move within a managed range against the US dollar. It scores 30 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and its weakest side, at 63, is corruption and secrecy around it. Two cases ended in convictions. On 31 January 2022 a court convicted former governor van Trikt of breaking the Anti-Corruption Act and of forgery, embezzlement, money laundering and taking part in a criminal enterprise, in a matter involving more than 800,000 US dollars taken at the bank's expense, and sentenced him to eight years in prison and a 500,000 Suriname dollar fine; the bank's legal director and others were convicted too, and on appeal in January 2026 his sentence was cut to six years. On 17 December 2021 a court sentenced Hoefdraad, who was not present, to 12 years and a fine of the same size for conspiring to defraud the bank while he was finance minister; on appeal on 19 January 2026 the court imposed 10 years for breaking the anti-corruption law and for embezzlement, and dropped the criminal-organisation count. Hoefdraad, who left Suriname in 2020, calls the case a political show trial. The bank holds 1.2 tonnes of gold and has three agreements with China to exchange currencies, signed on 18 March 2015, in 2017 and on 11 February 2019, though whether any of them is still in force is not known; one source records drawings of 988,182,600 renminbi in 2020. BDO Assurance NV audited its 2020 accounts, and notes have been printed by Giesecke+Devrient, an expansion of the initials the source gives rather than its own wording.
p:LBR: Liberia's money is the Liberian dollar, issued by the Central Bank of Liberia, which scores 30 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. In March 2019 a Monrovia court ordered former deputy governor Sirleaf, former governor Weeks and official Hagba held for trial on charges of economic sabotage, theft or misuse of public money and criminal conspiracy, over banknotes printed in 2016 to 2018 that could not be accounted for. The Justice Minister later dropped the charges against Sirleaf and three others, while Weeks remained under indictment, so nothing was proven against him. Crane Currency printed those notes under two contracts totalling 15 billion Liberian dollars, and a Presidential Investigation Team alleged it conspired with bank officials to print 18,151,000,000, beyond what was contracted; Crane denied wrongdoing and kickbacks and said it had not been charged, and the allegation is not a court finding. In July 2024 Liberia suspended governor Tarlue indefinitely after the General Auditing Commission reported on 2018 to 2023 and found irregularities in lending to the government, including more than 80 million US dollars in apparently unauthorised financing for salary payments, irregular contract awards and spending beyond approved limits; that stands as an official finding. The bank joined the World Bank's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership under a technical assistance agreement, described as training and advice rather than the partnership managing its assets. Deloitte & Touche in Accra and Baker Tilly Liberia in Monrovia audited the 2024 accounts.
p:COL: The Bank of the Republic issues Colombia's peso and prints it at its own banknote works; it is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, the bank used by central banks themselves. One case is recorded: in 2011 two officials were investigated for allegedly passing reserved information about people and companies to the DAS security agency and were suspended for a month, but in January 2011 the bank reported that the Procuraduria's ruling on appeal revoked the suspension, finding they had broken no rule. Government pressure was reported in 2 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, each time to cut rates. On 31 July 2025, after the board voted 4 to 3 to hold the rate at 9.25 per cent, President Gustavo Petro accused the bank of wanting to “finish off the economy” and of having an electoral bet. Amundi won a mandate in 2023, as one of eight outside managers, over 1.7 billion US dollars of its assets, and its reserve gold sits in the custody of the Bank of England, which is storage rather than management. Leonardo Villar became general manager in January 2021 after serving as an executive director at the International Monetary Fund.
p:MNE: The Central Bank of Montenegro does not issue money. Montenegro took the euro on its own: the Deutsche Mark became sole legal tender on 1 January 2001 and the euro replaced it in March 2002. The bank issues no euros and is not a member of the European System of Central Banks, but has a repo line, a short-term loan arrangement, of up to 250 million euros with the Eurosystem. It scores 33 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. Three cases are documented, all alleged and unproven. In July 2018 the bank's Council reportedly found that deputy governor Irena Radovic put personal interest ahead of the public interest and disclosed business secrets, and the bank asked parliament to dismiss her; she called the decision illegal retaliation and said she would sue, and no court has ruled. The NGO MANS said five payments totalling 4,100 euros went to relatives of governor Radoje Zugic in 2017 and 2018; he reportedly said he did not act illegally. In July 2012 MANS alleged to a prosecutor that First Bank got a 44 million euro state loan in 2008 it could not repay; no charge has been brought. “Ernst&Young Montenegro” Ltd Podgorica audits the bank's accounts.
p:COD: The Central Bank of the Congo issues the country's money. In April 2021 a report by Congo's state finance inspectorate, the IGF, called a 43 million US dollar transfer from a central bank account at BGFI Bank to the food importer Egal an embezzlement of public funds, and said the bank kept false accounts to cover it: its 2013 accounts showed about 43.1 million dollars in that account when the real balance was about 119,000 dollars. The former governor Deogratias Mutombo, the bank and PricewaterhouseCoopers did not respond to the journalists who reported this from leaked BGFI documents. On 25 October 2023 the accounts of Mutombo and of Albert Yuma, former board chairman of the mining company Gecamines, were frozen over an alleged embezzlement of 25.521 million dollars, with both men required to remain available to the national audit court; that allegation is unproven and still under investigation. Belgium's federal prosecutor also opened a money laundering investigation into Mutombo and five others, with searches in September 2023; as of October 2024 the prosecutor said no suspect had been charged. The bank scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Giesecke+Devrient printed the 200-franc note issued on 31 July 2007. The bank's accounts are audited by Ernst & Young RDC of Kinshasa, which gave an unqualified opinion on the year ended 31 December 2024.
p:NZL: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand issues the New Zealand dollar. It scores 23 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, less exposed than 91% of the 194 places scored, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it. On 10 March 2016 the decision on the Official Cash Rate, the interest rate the bank sets, leaked from its media lock-up before release. Deloitte, engaged on 11 March 2016 and reporting on 12 April 2016, traced it to a Mediaworks employee: one journalist emailed a draft story out of the lock-up, and another emailed the economics blogger Michael Reddell at 8.04am, before the 9am announcement. Mediaworks reported itself on 5 April 2016, and the bank ended embargoed lock-ups. Adrian Orr, governor from 27 March 2018, was chief economist at the bank Westpac in New Zealand from 2000 to 2003, joined the Reserve Bank as deputy governor in 2003, and ran the New Zealand Superannuation Fund from 2007 until his appointment. It part-owns the Bank for International Settlements, and Note Printing Australia prints its banknotes.
p:AFG: Da Afghanistan Bank is Afghanistan's central bank and issues the afghani. It scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, its weak point being corruption in the country, while the independence written into its law scores 0.87 of 1, where 1 means the bank holds the power. In May 2011 Afghanistan's High Office of Oversight and Anticorruption reported that the central bank had monitored Kabul Bank poorly; Kabul Bank had 925 million dollars in loans outstanding, many of them undocumented and given to powerful figures, before the central bank took it over in 2010. After the Taliban took power, the United States froze nearly 9.5 billion dollars of the bank's assets on 17 August 2021, much of it held at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, and stopped shipments of cash. On 11 February 2022 President Joe Biden signed an order splitting 7 billion dollars of the frozen money in two: 3.5 billion for relief in Afghanistan and 3.5 billion kept in the United States for lawsuits by US victims of terrorism. The bank holds 21.9 tonnes of gold, and its 2018 accounts were audited by Ernst & Young Ford Rhodes Sidat Hyder. A news report of 6 January 2020 said the bank had awarded the Polish Security Printing Works a contract for new 10, 20, 50 and 100 afghani notes, and on 1 February 2021 the Polish embassy in New Delhi announced that the works had delivered 380 million printed banknotes; no contract value is given and nothing says the arrangement continues.
p:UGA: The Bank of Uganda issues the Ugandan shilling, and the Auditor General audits its accounts. It scores 32 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 fully exposed, and its weakest side is corruption in the country. On paper it is among the less independent central banks, scoring 0.467 of 1 on a 42-rule measure of independence written into law. One case is recorded. A confidential 2018 Auditor General report to parliament said bank managers, including governor Mutebile, acted without guidelines, regulations or policies and may have intentionally neglected aspects of the closure and sale of at least seven commercial banks, including Crane Bank in 2016 and 2017. These are the findings of a report, not court verdicts. Sudhir Ruparelia, dfcu Bank and Nile River Acquisition Company are named in the case, the last two as having received money, favours or contracts from the central bank. Northern Trust supplies the bank with compliance, performance and risk analysis, and a dashboard for watching the outside firms that invest its money; that is analysis and advice, not management of the money.
p:MDV: The Maldives Monetary Authority issues the Maldivian rufiyaa, and its record turns on one scandal: the embezzlement of 1.3 billion rufiyaa from the Maldives Marketing and Public Relations Corporation. An Anti-Corruption Commission report made public in February 2019 found the authority negligent. Its Financial Intelligence Unit, the office that watches for suspicious money, was told in 2014 of a 59 million US dollar cheque from that company to a firm called SOF but did not look into it properly, did not examine SOF's large transactions through the Bank of Maldives and the Bank of Ceylon, and did not pass suspected money-laundering cases on. The unit's former head, Ibrahim Athif Shakoor, said governor Azeema Adam objected to filing a police report, citing too few staff and resources; Azeema said she had told him to investigate SOF's transactions and gave no specific instructions because the unit decided its own actions. In March 2019 police summoned governor Ahmed Naseer and confirmed he was being investigated for obstruction of justice, with no charge or court outcome named. He resigned in July 2019 amid allegations that he had got around the authority's rules and interfered in the unit's inquiries, one of them into a 22.5 million rufiyaa deposit to then-President Abdulla Yameen's account shortly before the 2018 election; Naseer denied influencing the unit and made counter-allegations, and no charges or findings followed. In February 2020 the Prosecutor General's Office charged Shakoor with negligence and failing to act appropriately on the case; he denied the allegations, and on 14 October 2025 that office withdrew the charge, citing how long it had been in court, with no conviction reported. Deloitte Partners in Male' audited the 2024 accounts. On 7 October 2024 India agreed a currency-borrowing line of 400 million US dollars and 30 billion Indian rupees. The authority scores 36 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:SGP: The Monetary Authority of Singapore is the central bank that issues the Singapore dollar. It scores 22 of 100 for outside influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 means fully exposed, making it less exposed than 93% of 194 places scored; its weakest side is that the country's laws hide who owns money. No documented case was found. Under a 1967 agreement, Brunei and Singapore accept each other's notes and coins at par. The bank is part-owner of the Bank for International Settlements, which 63 central banks own, and belongs to the Financial Stability Board. Former chairman Tharman Shanmugaratnam is a member of the Group of Thirty. It has 16 swap lines (agreements to borrow another central bank's currency). Note Printing Australia prints its banknotes. Ong Chong Tee, a Deputy Managing Director of the authority, was appointed a director of the commercial United Overseas Bank on 1 January 2023 and chairs its audit committee; he is also a director of AIA Group.
p:SRB: The National Bank of Serbia issues the Serbian dinar, and makes its own notes and coins at its Institute for Manufacturing Banknotes and Coins at Topčider, which has been operating since December 1929 and also produces for foreign countries. A bill, expected to pass on 15 July, would have placed the bank under government control and allowed the dismissal of governor Mladjan Dinkic: Prime Minister Zoran Djindjic wanted a devaluation Dinkic resisted, and members of the DOS coalition said a party official cannot be governor. Dinkic said the law would make the bank dependent on government and parliament; the authorities said his claims had no foundation. On 18 July 2003 he resigned, with two of the bank's three deputy governors, after parliament passed a law letting members of parliament nominate and appoint the bank's top officials; Energy Minister Kori Udovicki was nominated to succeed him. On 11 January 2006 police arrested vice-governor Dejan Simić, along with Vladimir Zagrađanin, on suspicion of taking bribes; an investigation was ordered and the bank's Council removed him on 16 January 2006, but no indictment, verdict or acquittal followed, so the suspicion is unproven. On 10 May 2011 Erste Bank Hungary named a former governor, Radovan Jelašić, its chairman and chief executive, to start that June. Serbia holds 54.6 tonnes of gold, is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, and scores 27 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:MNG: The Bank of Mongolia issues the tugrik. Two cases and two departures centre on N. Zoljargal, governor from 2012, who was replaced on 20 July 2016, two years before his term was due to end and with no reason given. The anti-corruption agency IAAC arrested him on 29 November 2017 over the Chinggis bond and a price-stabilising programme, part of a wider look at how the bank was run from 2012 to 2016; a court released him with a travel ban, prosecutors had not formally charged him and no later outcome was found, so nothing there is proven. In April 2020 he and three politicians were reported charged with abuse of power over illegally transferring 49 per cent of the Erdenet Mining Company; no outcome is recorded and those charges are unproven too. Lawmakers accepted the resignation of his successor, Nadmid Bayartsaikhan, on 21 November 2019, after the Financial Action Task Force, which sets international rules against money laundering, put Mongolia on its grey list over enforcement. The present governor, B. Lkhagvasuren, came from the World Bank in Washington to the bank as adviser to the governor in 2000, and the rest of his career is in Mongolian public bodies. Ernst & Young Mongolia Audit LLC audited the accounts for the 2020 financial year, and Giesecke & Devrient printed the new 5,000-togrog note. It holds two currency swap lines with China, arrangements to lend each other money, one renewed on 26 June 2026 at 15 billion yuan against 7.85 trillion tugrik, and scores 31 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:ECU: Ecuador uses the US dollar as its only legal tender, adopted in January 2000 at 25,000 sucres to the dollar, so the Central Bank of Ecuador issues no money of its own. It scores 31 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, its weak points being corruption in the country and the risk of money laundering in its banks. One case is recorded and it ended in conviction: on 8 January 2019 the National Court of Justice sentenced Pedro Delgado, a former president of the bank, to five years in prison, restitution of 788,855.94 dollars, forfeiture of assets and public apologies. Prosecutors described the crime as unlawful association while the court's own post called it illicit enrichment; the same source reports an earlier embezzlement conviction in 2015 carrying eight years, and says he allegedly allowed large loans without proper documents or guarantees while leading the bank, which is unproven. Government pressure was reported in 2 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, pressing the bank to loosen policy, change the law and print money. The bank joined the World Bank's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, described as giving it advice, executive training and asset-management expertise rather than a mandate to run Ecuador's reserves. Its 2021 accounts were audited by Kreston Audit Services Ecuador, and it holds 26.3 tonnes of gold, 27.7 percent of its reserves.
p:CMR: Cameroon's money, the Central African CFA franc, is issued by the Bank of Central African States (BEAC), which sets monetary policy for 6 members. The franc is fixed at EUR 1 = 655.957 CFA francs, France guarantees its convertibility, and the BEAC must keep at least 50% of its foreign reserves at the French Treasury. The bank scores 42 of 100 for outside influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 means fully exposed. One case is recorded: a November 2009 internal report found about 20 billion CFA francs diverted from the bank's Paris office to 139 beneficiaries between 2004 and 2008. On 28 September 2012 a court in Mfoundi sentenced Kemadjou to life imprisonment and ordered him to pay BEAC 26.4 billion CFA francs. Jean-Pierre Oyiba is named as a recipient of the money.
p:HKG: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority runs the Hong Kong dollar as a currency board, meaning it is tied to another currency: the monetary base is fully backed by US dollar assets in the Exchange Fund. The link began on 17 October 1983 at 7.80 Hong Kong dollars per US dollar, and since May 2005 the authority sells Hong Kong dollars at 7.75 and buys at 7.85. It scores 32 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. One case is recorded: in 2012 a Legislative Council subcommittee found that former chief Joseph Yam Chi-kwong should bear “ultimate responsibility” for investors' losses on Lehman's minibonds. The authority replied that the report had not fully taken into account the information it submitted, and some members prepared a minority report. Banknotes are printed in Hong Kong by Hong Kong Note Printing Limited, in which the government keeps management control and a majority stake.
p:SSD: South Sudan's money is the South Sudanese pound, issued by the Bank of South Sudan, and its notes are printed by De La Rue, which won a contract for 2.8 billion banknotes in 2011. The country scores 39 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, almost all of it from corruption in the country. A United Nations Human Rights Council commission report said De La Rue transferred about 1.4 million US dollars between 2016 and September 2017 into an Equity Bank account in Nairobi held by a consultant to the bank, against a banknote contract worth about 144 million dollars, and noted suspected corruption. That report stands as an official finding, but the United Kingdom's Serious Fraud Office, which opened its own investigation in July 2019, closed it in June 2020, saying the case did not meet the test for prosecution. On 9 June 2025 President Salva Kiir Mayardit removed Johnny Ohisa Domian as governor by decree, with no reason given; the first deputy governor, Addis Ababa Othow, replaced him. In February and March 2026 security forces detained former governor Manguak, placed under house arrest, with former finance ministers and other officials, and the information minister said a committee was investigating financial malpractices; no charges had been announced as of March 2026, so nothing is proven, and Manguak denies the allegations. The Auditor General audits the accounts.
p:ROU: The National Bank of Romania issues the Romanian leu, which in practice tracks the euro. It scores 22 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and no government pressure was reported from 2010 to 2018. One case is recorded. In 2014 the High Court of Cassation and Justice placed the sitting deputy governor, Olteanu, under 30-day house arrest in a National Anticorruption Directorate case alleging that in 2008, while parliament speaker, he asked for and received a 1 million euro bribe from the businessman Sorin Ovidiu Vantu. He was convicted of influence peddling and given a final five-year sentence in October 2020, but on 31 March 2023 the Bucharest Court of Appeal confirmed the case closed as time-barred and annulled the conviction, while ordering the money confiscated. The bank is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. Nicolae Danila ran Banca Comerciala Romana from 1999 to 2008, then sat on the bank's board until September 2014 and later chaired First Bank SA; no ethics finding is recorded. The bank said on 10 September 2024 that it is the holder of an account at the Bank of England where about 60 of its 103.6 tonnes of gold sit, that the custodian cannot use that gold in any form, and that transactions happen only on the bank's instruction; 42.4 tonnes are held in Romania. This reaches the record through a newspaper quoting the statement rather than through a document on the bank's own site.
p:MMR: The Central Bank of Myanmar issues the kyat, and the military has taken hold of its leadership. Three days after the coup of 1 February 2021 the military's State Administration Council made Than Than Swe a deputy governor; she later became governor in place of Than Nyein. In August 2022 the junta replaced Than Nyein and a vice chairman with Than Than Swe and Major General Zaw Myint Naing, two months after installing six lieutenant colonels as deputy directors. The former deputy governor Bo Bo Nge, arrested on the morning of the coup, was sentenced by a junta court in December 2022 to 20 years in prison after a months-long secret trial, which sources said concerned mismanagement of banks trading foreign currency; the junta-backed Anti-Corruption Commission accused him of not collecting tax on a 5 million US dollar Open Society deposit and of placing a 350 million dollar loan in a lower-interest account. Those accusations are the commission's own, and the economist Sean Turnell called Bo Bo Nge someone fighting against corruption. Government pressure was reported in 18 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, mostly pressing the bank to ease and to print money. Giesecke+Devrient of Munich, which had supplied raw materials and system components for printing kyat notes, suspended all deliveries to the state-owned Security Print Works after the military crackdown. The bank's own printing works at Wazi printed a 20,000-kyat commemorative note introduced on 31 July 2023, which is not the circulating series. Myanmar scores 55 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, third of the 194 places scored.
p:KNA: St Kitts and Nevis does not issue its own money. The East Caribbean dollar is issued by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank, set up under an agreement signed on 5 July 1983, for eight member places, and the rate has been held at 2.70 East Caribbean dollars to one US dollar since July 1976, when the peg moved from sterling. The country scores 29 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, its weakest side being corruption and secrecy around it, and no government pressure on the bank was reported in any of the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case concerns the bank: after it seized the Stanford-owned Bank of Antigua, the Official Stanford Investors Committee sued it in Dallas in 2013, alleging it had fraudulently taken assets belonging to Stanford's victims and creditors; on 17 August 2018 a US federal judge dismissed the claims in full because the bank and Antigua are immune under US foreign sovereign immunity law, without ruling on whether the allegations were true. Trevor Brathwaite, an accountant who earlier worked for KPMG Peat Marwick, was deputy governor from April 2006 to September 2021 and sat on the board of East Caribbean Financial Holding Co. Ltd, a financial holding company; no dates are given for that seat, and the move is not an accusation. De La Rue prints the notes and PricewaterhouseCoopers Eastern Caribbean audits the accounts.
p:GTM: The Bank of Guatemala issues the quetzal and in practice holds it close to a fixed rate against the US dollar. One case is recorded. In May 2015 the bank's president, Julio Suarez, was arrested along with other members of the board of the social security institute, the IGSS. Prosecutors said the group took part in the irregular award of a 116 million quetzal IGSS contract, about 14.5 million US dollars, to the drug company Pisa de Guatemala, on charges of unlawful association, influence peddling, illegal commissions and active bribery. He was acquitted on appeal in June 2019, and the Supreme Court's Criminal Chamber upheld that acquittal, as reported in October 2021. No government pressure was reported from 2010 to 2018. The bank keeps coined gold worth about 315.5 million US dollars at the end of 2024 in its own vaults, and gold worth about 263.1 million dollars in storage at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, which holds it while Guatemala still owns it. Its smaller notes are printed abroad: on 20 August 2018 the bank agreed with the Polish printer Polska Wytwornia Papierow Wartosciowych to produce 5- and 10-quetzal notes on a material containing synthetic fibres. It is also a member of the World Bank Treasury's RAMP network, which offers advice, training and asset management, without saying which of those Guatemala gets. Guatemala scores 32 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:CIV: Côte d'Ivoire uses the West African CFA franc, issued by the Central Bank of West African States, the BCEAO, which sets monetary policy for eight member countries. The franc is pegged — held at a fixed rate — at 655.957 to the euro, and France promises to advance euros if the bank's reserves run out; a 2019 agreement ended the rule that it keep at least half its reserves at the French Treasury. The country scores 39 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. Two cases come out of the post-election crisis of December 2010 to April 2011. On 18 January 2018 a court sentenced Laurent Gbagbo, Aké N'Gbo, Katinan and Dallo to 20 years and a fine of 329 billion CFA francs for offences including group theft by break-in of BCEAO vaults and cash; seven bailiffs got 36 months and a 700,000 CFA franc fine, Katinan was absent throughout, Gbagbo always denied the charges, and on 6 August 2022 President Ouattara pardoned him. Earlier, in January 2011, a summit of UEMOA heads of state accepted governor Dacoury-Tabley's resignation, after he was criticized for ignoring a 23 December decision by UEMOA finance ministers that gave Alassane Ouattara power over the institution; the account says the bank paid 60 to 100 billion CFA francs to the Gbagbo regime after that date, and Senegal's President Abdoulaye Wade asked for an audit and alleged 500 billion CFA francs had been moved, with no audit result given.
p:SEN: Senegal uses the West African CFA franc, issued for eight countries by the Central Bank of West African States, the BCEAO, which is based in Senegal. The franc is fixed at 655.957 to the euro, and the French Treasury promises to advance euros if the bank's reserves run out; an agreement signed on 21 December 2019 ended the rule that at least half those reserves sit at the Treasury. One case is recorded. In January 2011 a summit of UEMOA heads of state accepted governor Dacoury-Tabley's resignation, after he was criticized for ignoring a 23 December decision by UEMOA finance ministers that gave Alassane Ouattara power over the institution; the report says the BCEAO paid out 60 to 100 billion CFA francs to the Gbagbo regime afterwards. President Abdoulaye Wade asked for an audit and alleged the former governor moved 500 billion CFA francs to Gbagbo; that is unproven, and no audit result is given.
p:CAN: The Bank of Canada issues the Canadian dollar, which moves within a band of 2% or less against the US dollar. Canada scores 20 of 100 on exposure to influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 means fully exposed; that is 187th of 194, among the least exposed. No documented case at the bank was found, and no government pressure was reported from 2010 to 2018. The bank’s own profile of Mark Carney, governor from 1 February 2008 to 1 June 2013, describes a thirteen-year career at the investment bank Goldman Sachs, in its London, Tokyo, New York and Toronto offices, before he entered the public service. It is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. EY and PwC audit its accounts, and Canadian Bank Note Company and BA International print its notes. The Canadian dollar is 5.76% of world currency trading and 2.47% of foreign reserves, and the bank has 9 swap lines, which are agreements to borrow another central bank's currency.
p:AGO: The National Bank of Angola issues the kwanza (AOA). Angola scores 41 of 100 on exposure to influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 means fully exposed; its weakest side is secrecy about who owns money and corruption (index score 32 of 100). Government pressure was reported in 29 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, nearly all pressing the bank to cut rates or ease, with 8 threats to replace leaders. On 14 August 2020 the Supreme Court convicted former governor Valter Filipe (eight years), BNA manager Samalia (five years), José Filomeno dos Santos (five years) and businessman Sebastião (six years) of embezzlement, fraud and influence peddling over an attempted transfer of $500 million to a London account, which a British bank blocked. The Constitutional Court is also named in the case. Goznak, the Russian state printer, printed the 5,000-kwanza note.
p:PER: The Central Reserve Bank of Peru issues the sol, managed within a band of about 5 per cent against the US dollar, and Peru scores 25 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. One matter, from 1986 to 1991, is alleged and unproven. A New York grand-jury indictment of the Bank of Credit and Commerce International in 1991 alleged three million US dollars in bribes in return for depositing part of Peru's 1986-87 reserves in that bank's Panama branch, after the Peruvian board approved moving 100 million dollars and later doubling it. The indictment named no officials of the Peruvian bank; the Christian Science Monitor identified Figueroa and Neyra, and both strenuously denied the charges, Neyra calling the decision purely technical. All Peruvian deposits were withdrawn by the end of 1987, and a Peruvian parliamentary commission also looked into the bank. Separately, Eduardo Torres-Llosa spent 21 years at BBVA in Peru, left in June 2019 as its managing director, sat on the boards of Financiera Confianza and BBVA in Uruguay and chaired the engineering firm Cosapi, and became the central bank's general manager in March 2022; no ethics finding is recorded. The bank is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. Perum Peruri won the tender to print the 10, 20 and 50 nuevo sol notes, reported as still unsigned in January 2020 and as secured by December 2022, with no value given, and a member firm of PricewaterhouseCoopers audits the accounts.
p:SLE: The Bank of Sierra Leone issues the leone and scores 36 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed; its weakest side is corruption and secrecy, at 66. Under the 2019 Bank of Sierra Leone Act, sacking the governor needs a two-thirds majority in parliament. In August 2018 the recently elected president dismissed the governor, and Kelfala Kallon was appointed on 15 August as the bank's third governor in 17 months; neither the dismissed governor nor either side's reason is named. On 22 November 2021 Kallon told parliament that he had bribed people hoarding the leone to bring it back into the banking system. The Anti-Corruption Commission investigated and said in May 2022 that he had meant cash swap operations in which the bank sold about 68.6 million United States dollars of foreign currency in 2021, that the word was used in error, and that it had closed the investigation after advising him to choose his words more carefully. On 13 March 2023 President Julius Maada Bio sent Kallon on indefinite leave and named his deputy, Ibrahim Stevens, interim head; no official reason was given, Kallon did not respond, and the president was reported to be bypassing the 2019 Act. De La Rue printed the 10-leone note of the redenominated series introduced on 1 July 2022, and the West African Monetary Institute manages the Stabilization and Cooperation Fund, in which the bank holds 63.59 million new leone.
p:TZA: The Bank of Tanzania issues the Tanzanian shilling. It scores 31 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and government pressure on it was reported in 2 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018. An audit by Ernst & Young of the bank's External Payment Arrears account found about 133 billion shillings paid out wrongly in 2005 and 2006 to 22 local companies, many phoney or using fake documents. President Jakaya Kikwete dismissed governor Ballali in January 2008, the companies were ordered to refund the money, and some lower-level defendants were jailed. In the first court cases to follow, reported on 27 May 2011, the Kisutu Resident Magistrate's Court in Dar es Salaam convicted the businessmen Farijala Hussein and Rajabu Maranda of offences related to financial impropriety, forgery and obtaining credit under false pretences, jailed them for five years and ordered them to return what they had taken. The bank is also audited by the Controller and Auditor General, and in 2024 the printing firms De La Rue and Crane Currency won its tender to reprint its banknotes.
p:YEM: The Central Bank of Yemen issues the rial, held close to a fixed rate against the US dollar. It scores 43 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and the corruption and secrecy around it stand at 86. Government pressure was reported in 6 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, all of it pressing for easier money or for printing money. On 18 September 2016 President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi, announcing from Saudi Arabia, sacked central bank head Mohammed bin Hammam, named Mansar al-Kaiti in his place and ordered the bank moved to Aden, with no official reason given. On 6 December 2021 he dismissed the governor and his deputy, the fourth such sacking since the civil war began. A UN Panel of Experts report in January 2021 said the Aden-based bank broke its foreign-exchange rules and laundered 'a substantial part' of a 2 billion dollar Saudi deposit, giving traders a 423 million dollar windfall. The bank rejected the claims, and on 25 March 2021, after an internal review, the panel withdrew the money-laundering and corruption accusations.
p:TUN: The Central Bank of Tunisia issues the dinar, which follows a slowly adjusted fixed rate against the euro. On 27 June 2012 President Moncef Marzouki fired the governor, Mustapha Kamel Nabli, saying he had refused to bring monetary policy in line with the country's economic needs; the elected assembly approved the removal in July 2012. In February 2018 Tunisian prosecutors said five of the bank's agents had been arrested, two of them jailed, in a currency-trafficking investigation. They were accused of money laundering, corruption and abuse of power for exchanging small euro notes for 200- and 500-euro notes without recording the exchanges, and the bank said it had referred the operations to the courts itself. They stand charged and the accusations are unproven. The bank's 2025 accounts were audited jointly by FMBZ - KPMG Tunisie and Cabinet C.M.C, it holds 6.8 tonnes of gold, and Tunisia scores 28 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Oberthur Fiduciaire, printed in the source under its former name Oberthur Technologies, printed the 20-dinar note.
p:LSO: Lesotho issues the loti, and the South African rand circulates alongside it. Under the Common Monetary Area, which replaced a Rand Monetary Area agreement signed in December 1974 and was followed by a Multilateral Monetary Agreement in February 1992 when Namibia joined, member currencies are pegged to the rand one for one and are legal tender only in the country that issues them; Lesotho must back what it issues fully with rand assets, and South Africa pays it an imputed return on rand circulating there. All five of its current notes, introduced on 23 December 2021, are printed by De La Rue. In February 2024 three South Africans appeared in the Ficksburg Magistrates Court on fraud and money laundering charges over 57 million rand said to have been stolen from the Central Bank of Lesotho. The Hawks, a South African police unit, said Lesotho officials intercepted vouchers meant for service providers and diverted the payments to co-conspirators in South Africa, and that some officials were already before court in Lesotho. The charges are unproven. Its 2023 accounts were audited by Moteane, Quashie & Associates with SizweNtsalubaGobodo Grant Thornton. Lesotho scores 30 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and corruption and secrecy around the bank is its weakest side, at 60.
p:KGZ: The National Bank of the Kyrgyz Republic issues the som and holds it within 2 per cent of the US dollar. One case is recorded. In September 2005 prosecutors placed the governor, Ulan Sarbanov, under house arrest, accusing him of abuse of power for handing more than 400,000 US dollars to the deposed president Askar Akayev in 1999. Sarbanov denied wrongdoing, and Euromoney reported that his position had been insecure since Akayev was ousted in March 2005. On 26 April 2006 Judge Esenjan Abylkasymov acquitted him and four other former finance officials, ruling that there was no crime because they had acted in the interests of the state; the prosecutor's office said it would appeal, and no appeal outcome was found. Two heads have left since: parliament approved the early resignation of Kubanychbek Bokontaev on 26 June 2024, and Melis Turgunbaev, chairman from that same day, resigned on 18 March 2026, which the report calls voluntary. Neither article gives a reason. Crane Currency printed the 5,000-som note introduced on 10 May 2024; Central Asian Secure Printing Typography began printing at home in September 2026, with 20- and 50-som notes entering circulation on 27 October, while an earlier attempt by Uchkun in March 2025 produced 10-som notes that never circulated. Kyrgyzstan scores 31 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:NAM: The Bank of Namibia is the country's central bank. Namibia belongs to the Common Monetary Area with South Africa, Lesotho and Eswatini, joining under the agreement of February 1992: the Namibian dollar is pegged to the South African rand one for one, and every Namibian dollar issued must be fully backed by rand assets. The bank scores 26 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and the law gives it middling independence, 0.637 of 1 and 103rd of 155 countries. In 2002 court papers in a suit by Nambib Resources against the Minister of Mines listed governor Tom Alweendo as a 10 per cent shareholder in Trade Line Namibia, which held an exclusive licence to prospect on the Skeleton Coast. Alweendo said he had been made a director without his knowledge, and no finding or outcome is reported, so the allegation is unproven. Johannes !Gawaxab came from a private-sector banking career to the governorship on 1 June 2020, succeeding Ipumbu Shiimi; the bank's board page now shows Ebson Uanguta as governor from 1 January 2026. Deloitte Namibia and Grand Namibia audit its accounts, and De La Rue printed its new 50-dollar note.
p:KHM: The National Bank of Cambodia is the country's central bank. It scores 36 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and neither matter on record was ever confirmed. The Phnom Penh Post reported that governor Thor Peng Leath lent three million US dollars of central bank money on 31 May 1994 so Credit Bank of Cambodia could meet its minimum capital, which bank officials admitted was highly irregular, and that on 8 May 1995 the bank released 145,000 dollars from former commerce minister Var Huot's frozen account. Preferential treatment was claimed, but Var Huot said there was none, and no charges or findings followed. In November 2013 Chea Serey, daughter of governor Chea Chanto, was promoted to director-general; former deputy governor Tioulong Saumura said being the governor's daughter should exclude her, Nguon Sokha called her a skilled technocrat, and no investigation followed. The bank belongs to the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, which central banks join for help with their reserves. BNY Mellon supplies it with reporting systems and staff training.
p:BLR: The National Bank of the Republic of Belarus issues the Belarusian ruble and holds it within 2 percent of a mix of the euro, the Russian ruble and the US dollar. It scores 31 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. In December 2016 the state security service, the KGB, said a directorate head at the bank and his deputy had been arrested over a bribe, reported as 13,000 dollars, for choosing the company BelAVM as an equipment supplier; the matter is unproven. At a trial reported in March 2020 prosecutors charged Feliks Kasperovich and Andrei Podgorny of the bank's information technology directorate with taking at least $868,750 in bribes from 2007 onwards, and Igor Kudasov, head of its payment systems directorate, with taking $30,000. Kasperovich admitted the charges in full; the rest remains unproven. Belarus also has two agreements with China, from 2010 and 2015, to borrow its currency. The China Banknote Printing and Minting Corporation printed the 80-ruble commemorative note introduced on 31 March 2025.
p:GMB: The Central Bank of The Gambia issues the dalasi and scores 30 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. The Janneh Commission, a public inquiry into the finances of former president Yahya Jammeh, found that governor Amadou Colley had let Jammeh and General Sulayman Badjie take money out without proper authorisation, including millions of dollars by Badjie. Appearing before that commission on 19 September 2017, Colley said accounts controlled by the Office of the President had been opened at the bank, that an account for sand mining was opened at that office's request, which he called irregular, and that withdrawals followed instructions from someone in the office without the account signatory's approval. The government's White Paper on the inquiry accepted that between September 2015 and January 2017 Badjie, purportedly acting for Jammeh, instructed the governor or his deputies to release US dollars, and that cash was handed over by the governor to soldiers and loaded into vehicles. It held Badjie accountable for $15,785,601, 300,000 euros and 9,606,000 dalasi and ordered the money recovered by forfeiting and selling his properties, and it also records $28.5 million illegally granted in one bank account in 2000 and 2001 and $268,000 stolen from the bank and used to buy the Observer newspaper. Colley was banned from holding public office for life and held jointly liable for the money taken in breach of the bank's procedures. De La Rue has printed notes for the bank, and PKF Gambia and PKF Nigeria audited the 2021 accounts.
p:MUS: The Bank of Mauritius issues the Mauritian rupee and holds it within about 2 per cent of the United States dollar. Mauritius scores 25 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and 0.733 of 1 on an index of independence in law, where 1 means the bank rather than the government holds the power. On 9 and 10 April 2025 the country's Financial Crimes Commission arrested the former governor, Seegolam, for fraud by abuse of position; he was charged with fraud and released on bail. The investigation concerns the alleged taking of 300 million rupees, about 6.7 million United States dollars, from the Mauritius Investment Corporation, a vehicle owned by the central bank and set up during the COVID pandemic. Seegolam and Renganaden Padayachy deny wrongdoing, and the charge is unproven. Rama Krishna Sithanen became governor on 16 November 2024, the day after he stopped chairing the fund administration firm Apex Group (Mauritius); he had chaired Sanne Mauritius from 2017 to 2022 and International Financial Services from 2011 to 2016. That is a career move, not an accusation. The bank holds 12.4 tonnes of gold, with bars in storage at the Bank of England.
p:ISL: The Central Bank of Iceland issues the króna and keeps it within 2 per cent or less of the euro. It scores 16 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, lower than 99 per cent of the 194 places with a figure, and it ranks 9th of 112 for what it tells the public. No government pressure on it was reported in any of the 37 quarters covered between 2010 and 2018. One case is on its record, an official finding: in April 2010, after the 2008 collapse of Iceland's three largest banks, parliament's Special Investigation Commission found that seven officials, among them central bank head Oddsson and officials Gudnason and Fridriksson, had acted with gross negligence by failing to act on information about the banks' condition. The bank is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, the bank for central banks.
p:DNK: Danmarks Nationalbank issues the Danish krone and holds it at a rate against the euro that is announced in advance. At the end of 2025 it held assets of 109.8 billion US dollars. It is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, the bank used by central banks, and PwC signed the auditor's report on its 2025 accounts. Oberthur Fiduciaire was chosen as banknote supplier under a four-year framework, with the first notes in circulation in 2020, and the bank has since agreed with De La Rue to produce a new Danish series at De La Rue's plant outside London, due for launch in 2028 under a contract running at least six years. It can borrow foreign currency under two swap lines: up to 30 billion US dollars from the United States, agreed on 19 March 2020 as a temporary pandemic facility and expired on 31 December 2021, and a standing 24,000 million euros from the European Central Bank. Since 2002 about 97 per cent of its roughly 66.5 tonnes of gold has been kept at the Bank of England in London and about 0.5 per cent at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, with about 2.5 per cent in Copenhagen; those are storage arrangements, not management. Lars Rohde, who chaired the Board of Governors from 2013 to 2023, had worked at the mortgage bank Realkredit Danmark until 1998 and then ran the statutory pension body ATP; he joined the board of the bank Nordea in 2024, and no ethics finding is recorded. Denmark scores 16 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:BWA: The Bank of Botswana issues the pula, which it manages against the South African rand, moving the rate in small steps within a narrow band. One case is recorded and it ended in acquittal. A woman arrested on 17 October 2019 was accused, with others including former president Ian Khama and former intelligence head Isaac Kgosi, of stealing 100 billion pula from the bank. High Court judge Zein Kebonang discharged and acquitted her of unexplained property and a false passport declaration, the state withdrew a terrorism financing charge, and he found the accusations fabricated and referred the investigator to police for perjury prosecution. The accusations against the others remain unproven. Northern Trust works for the bank on measuring and explaining how its investments have performed and on training staff, which the source describes as reporting and training rather than management of its assets. The 10 pula polymer note that entered circulation on 1 February 2018 was designed and printed by De La Rue. EY audits the accounts. Botswana scores 23 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed.
p:KWT: The Central Bank of Kuwait issues the Kuwaiti dinar and holds it at a fixed rate against the US dollar announced in advance. Its assets were 36.4 billion US dollars at the end of 2025, and it is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. Two accounting firms check its books, Al-Aiban, Al-Osaimi & Partners of Ernst & Young and KPMG, Safi Al-Mutawa & Partners, which signed off the accounts for the fiscal year ended 31 March 2013, and Note Printing Australia's customer list says it has produced and supplied polymer banknotes to the bank. One case is recorded and it is unproven: the Kuwaiti newspaper Al Jarida, citing unnamed sources, reported that the securities regulator had decided to refer Governor Mohammad Al Hashel to prosecutors over a suspected breach of investment rules involving shares in a local bank. He denied it, saying he had never traded shares in a listed company while in senior posts; the regulator did not answer Reuters' calls. Governor Basel Al-Haroon, in post since April 2022, worked at the bank from 1989 to 2006 and from late 2006 to 2012, and in between and afterwards led a Kuwaiti investment company and was vice chairman of a Kuwaiti bank from 2016 to 2018. No ethics finding is recorded. Kuwait scores 32 of 100, and 3 of 15 on how much it tells the public.
p:EGY: The Central Bank of Egypt issues the Egyptian pound, which it keeps within 2 percent or less of the US dollar, and prints its own notes at its Banknote Printing House in the New Administrative Capital. Egypt scores 31 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. Government pressure was reported in 1 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, a threat to replace leaders. In October 2015 Daily News Egypt reported that severe pressure, from no named source, pushed governor Hisham Ramez out a month early; that is unconfirmed. On 17 August 2022 governor Tarek Amer, whose term was due to run to 2023, resigned; President al-Sisi accepted it and made him a presidential adviser, with the pound at 19.1 to the dollar. His successor Hassan Abdalla had been vice chairman and managing director of the Arab African International Bank from 2002 to 2018. No documented case of wrongdoing was found.
p:SOM: Somalia's money is the Somali shilling, and the Central Bank of Somalia issues it, though the notes are printed abroad: the circulating 2,000-shilling note comes from Sudan's state currency printing works. Two cases are recorded. In 2013 governor Abrar resigned after seven weeks, writing to the president that from her appointment she had continuously been asked to sanction deals and violate her fiduciary responsibility; she had refused to sanction a contract over frozen government assets with the United States law firm Shulman Rogers, which denied wrongdoing. A July 2013 report by the United Nations Monitoring Group for Somalia and Eritrea, an official finding, said 80 per cent of withdrawals from the bank were made for private purposes, that the governor was key to the irregularities, and that 12 million of 16.9 million US dollars transferred by the accounting firm PricewaterhouseCoopers could not be traced; the bank rejected the allegations. The bank later joined the World Bank's Reserves Advisory and Management Program, described in its own newsletter as technical support and advice rather than management of its assets. Somalia scores 37 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:GNQ: Equatorial Guinea uses the Central African CFA franc (XAF), issued by the Bank of Central African States (BEAC), which sets monetary policy for 6 members. The franc is fixed at EUR 1 = 655.957 CFA francs. France guarantees convertibility without limit, and the BEAC must deposit at least 50% of its foreign exchange reserves at the French Treasury (lowered from 65% in 2007). Exposure score is 46 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed. The BEAC scores 0.5 of 15 on transparency, last of 112, and government pressure to cut rates or ease was reported in 3 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case: a November 2009 internal report found about 20 billion CFA francs diverted from the Paris office to 139 beneficiaries between 2004 and 2008. On 28 September 2012 a court in Mfoundi, Cameroon, sentenced Kemadjou to life imprisonment and ordered him to pay BEAC 26.4 billion CFA francs.
p:NIC: Nicaragua's money is issued by the Central Bank of Nicaragua, which scores 29 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. One case runs from 2000 to 2008 and ended in an official finding. In 2007 the country's Comptroller General, the state auditor, concluded that the bank's board sold CENI certificates, paper issued to cover the collapse of banks, for less than they were worth and then raised interest rates to the benefit of the main buyer, Bancentro; the fraud is put at 500 million dollars. The Comptroller alleged criminal involvement by six men, among them former finance minister Eduardo Montealegre, who denied wrongdoing and called it a political witch hunt, and in July 2008 a special prosecutor filed charges against 39 people including him. No central bank officials are named among the accused and no court ruling is given, though former bank president Francisco Mayorga had already been found guilty in the banking scandal. Baker Tilly Nicaragua, S.A. audited the accounts for 2024, and on 27 March 2024 the printer Orell Fussli was reported to have been partly awarded a tender to print and supply the bank's banknotes, with no value or quantity given.
p:CAF: The Central African Republic uses the Central African CFA franc (XAF), issued by the Bank of Central African States (BEAC), which sets monetary policy for 6 members. The franc is fixed at EUR 1 = 655.957 CFA francs. France guarantees convertibility without limit, and the BEAC must deposit at least 50% of its foreign exchange reserves at the French Treasury (lowered from 65% in 2007). Exposure score is 45 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed. The BEAC scores 0.5 of 15 on transparency, last of 112, and government pressure to cut rates or ease was reported in 3 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case: a November 2009 internal report found about 20 billion CFA francs diverted from the Paris office to 139 beneficiaries between 2004 and 2008. On 28 September 2012 a court in Mfoundi, Cameroon, sentenced Kemadjou to life imprisonment and ordered him to pay BEAC 26.4 billion CFA francs.
p:COG: Congo-Brazzaville uses the XAF, issued by the Bank of Central African States (BEAC), which sets monetary policy for 6 members. The XAF is pegged, meaning held at a fixed rate, at EUR 1 = 655.957 CFA francs, and France guarantees to supply euros if the region cannot pay for imports. On the map's scale, 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed; Congo-Brazzaville scores 45, more exposed than 91% of places with a figure, mainly from corruption in the country and money-laundering risk. One BEAC case is documented: a November 2009 internal report found about 20 billion CFA francs diverted from its Paris office to 139 beneficiaries between 2004 and 2008, and on 28 September 2012 a court in Mfoundi, Cameroon, sentenced Kemadjou to life imprisonment and ordered him to pay BEAC 26.4 billion CFA francs.
p:TCD: Chad uses the XAF, issued by the Bank of Central African States (BEAC), which sets monetary policy for 6 members. The XAF is pegged, meaning held at a fixed rate, at EUR 1 = 655.957 CFA francs, and France guarantees to supply euros if the region cannot pay for imports. On the map's scale, 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed; Chad scores 45, more exposed than 92% of places with a figure, mainly from corruption in the country and money-laundering risk. One BEAC case is documented: a November 2009 internal report found about 20 billion CFA francs diverted from its Paris office to 139 beneficiaries between 2004 and 2008, and on 28 September 2012 a court in Mfoundi, Cameroon, sentenced Kemadjou to life imprisonment and ordered him to pay BEAC 26.4 billion CFA francs.
p:GAB: Gabon uses the XAF, issued by the Bank of Central African States (BEAC), which sets monetary policy for 6 members. The XAF is pegged, meaning held at a fixed rate, at EUR 1 = 655.957 CFA francs, and France guarantees to supply euros if the region cannot pay for imports. On the map's scale, 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed; Gabon scores 44, more exposed than 89% of places with a figure, mainly from money-laundering risk and corruption in the country. One BEAC case is documented: a November 2009 internal report found about 20 billion CFA francs diverted from its Paris office to 139 beneficiaries between 2004 and 2008, and on 28 September 2012 a court in Mfoundi, Cameroon, sentenced Kemadjou to life imprisonment and ordered him to pay BEAC 26.4 billion CFA francs.
p:GNB: Guinea-Bissau uses the West African CFA franc, issued by the Central Bank of West African States, the BCEAO, which sets monetary policy for eight member countries. The franc is pegged — held at a fixed rate — at one euro to 655.957 CFA francs, and France gives an unconditional, unlimited promise to advance euros if the bank's reserves run out. An agreement signed in Abidjan on 21 December 2019 replaced the 1973 one: it ended the requirement that the bank keep at least half its reserves at the French Treasury, and France withdrew its representatives from the board, the Monetary Policy Committee and the banking commission, though one independent committee member is still appointed in consultation with the French government. Guinea-Bissau scores 44 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, mostly because of corruption in the country and money-laundering risk in its banks. One case is documented: in January 2011 a summit of UEMOA heads of state accepted governor Dacoury-Tabley's resignation, after he was criticized for ignoring a 23 December decision by UEMOA finance ministers that gave Alassane Ouattara power over the institution; the account says the bank paid 60 to 100 billion CFA francs to the Gbagbo regime after that date, and Senegal's President Abdoulaye Wade asked for an audit and alleged the former governor moved 500 billion CFA francs to Gbagbo after being dismissed, with no audit result given.
