p:MLI: Mali's money is the CFA franc, issued not by a national central bank but by the Central Bank of West African States, known as the BCEAO, which sets monetary policy for eight member countries. The rate is fixed at 1 euro to 655.957 CFA francs, and France gives an unconditional, unlimited guarantee that the currency can be exchanged, advancing money to the bank if its foreign currency reserves run out. A cooperation agreement signed in Abidjan on 21 December 2019 replaced the 1973 one and ended the requirement that the bank keep at least half its reserves at the French Treasury; the bank's account there was closed in April 2021 according to a French Senate report, while the Treasury's own page says there has been no such account since January 2020. France approved the agreement by a law of 3 February 2021 and withdrew its representatives from the bank's board, its Monetary Policy Committee and the regional banking commission, though one independent member of that committee is still appointed in consultation with the French government. The agreement provides for the currency to be renamed the eco, and a West African meeting on 7 September 2026 kept 2027 as the target year for launching a single currency of that name. Mali scores 41 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, mainly because of corruption in the country and the risk of money laundering. One case is recorded at the bank: a summit of heads of state accepted governor Dacoury-Tabley's resignation in January 2011 after he was criticised for ignoring a decision of 23 December by the union's finance ministers that handed control of the institution to Alassane Ouattara, and the report says the bank paid out 60 to 100 billion CFA francs to the Gbagbo regime after that date. Senegal's President Abdoulaye Wade called for an audit and alleged that the former governor moved 500 billion CFA francs to Gbagbo after being dismissed; another figure given is 300 billion, and no audit result is reported. Its accounts are checked by firms appointed in pairs, one the titulaire that does the audit and the other the suppléant that stands in: Grant Thornton Senegal with a grouping of PKF BAGE and Crowe TG ICAAF behind it, and Deloitte Côte d'Ivoire with Mazars Senegal behind it for 2024 to 2029.
p:BFA: Burkina Faso uses the West African CFA franc, issued by the Central Bank of West African States, the BCEAO, which sets monetary policy for eight member countries. The franc is pegged, meaning held at a fixed rate, at one euro to 655.957 CFA francs, and France promises to advance euros if the bank's reserves run out; an agreement signed on 21 December 2019 ended the requirement that at least half those reserves sit at the French Treasury. One case is recorded: a summit of UEMOA heads of state accepted governor Dacoury-Tabley's resignation in January 2011, after he was criticized for ignoring a 23 December decision by UEMOA finance ministers that gave Alassane Ouattara power over the institution, and the article says the BCEAO paid out 60 to 100 billion CFA francs to the Gbagbo regime afterwards. Abdoulaye Wade asked for an audit and alleged the former governor moved 500 billion CFA francs to Gbagbo; that is unproven.
p:NER: Niger uses the CFA franc, issued by the Central Bank of West African States (BCEAO), which sets monetary policy for 8 members. The currency is pegged, held at a fixed rate of 1 euro to 655.957 CFA francs, and the French Treasury guarantees, without condition or limit, to advance euros if the BCEAO's reserves run out. A cooperation agreement signed on 21 December 2019 ended the requirement that the BCEAO keep at least 50% of its reserves at the French Treasury. Niger scores 41 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, mainly from money-laundering risk and corruption in the country. The BCEAO has one documented case: a summit of UEMOA heads of state accepted governor Dacoury-Tabley's resignation in January 2011, after he was criticized for ignoring a 23 December decision by finance ministers giving Alassane Ouattara power over the institution; reports say the BCEAO paid 60 to 100 billion CFA francs to the Gbagbo regime after that date. Senegal's President Wade asked for an audit and alleged the former governor moved 500 billion CFA francs to Gbagbo; another figure given is 300 billion, and no audit result is reported. Mazars Niger was selected to audit the BCEAO's accounts for 2024 to 2029.
p:BEN: Benin does not have its own central bank. Its money is the West African CFA franc, issued by the Central Bank of West African States, known by its French initials BCEAO, which sets monetary policy for eight member countries. The franc is pegged, meaning held at a fixed rate, at one euro to 655.957 CFA francs, and France guarantees, without condition or limit, to advance euros if the BCEAO's reserves run out. A cooperation agreement signed in Abidjan on 21 December 2019 replaced the 1973 one and ended the requirement that the BCEAO keep at least half its reserves at the French Treasury, and France withdrew its representatives from the BCEAO board, its Monetary Policy Committee and the banking commission, though one independent committee member is still appointed in consultation with the French government. Benin scores 38 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, mainly from money-laundering risk in its banks and corruption in the country. One case is documented at the central bank: a summit of regional heads of state accepted governor Dacoury-Tabley's resignation in January 2011, after he was criticised for ignoring a 23 December decision by the union's finance ministers giving Alassane Ouattara power over the institution, and the account says the BCEAO paid out 60 to 100 billion CFA francs to the Gbagbo regime after that date. Senegal's President Abdoulaye Wade asked for an audit and alleged the former governor moved 500 billion CFA francs, or by another figure 300 billion, to Gbagbo after being dismissed; no audit result is reported, so that is unproven. The accounts are audited by firms appointed in pairs, one doing the work and one standing in: Deloitte Benin with Mazars Benin for Benin, and Deloitte Cote d'Ivoire with Mazars Senegal for the BCEAO itself.
p:BIH: The convertible mark is issued by the Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina under a currency board: marks are put into circulation only against convertible foreign currency the bank holds, at 1.95583 marks to the euro, and its monetary liabilities may never exceed its foreign currency assets. It is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, and it has joined the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, which offers advice, training and asset management, with the announcement stating the membership rather than which of those services the bank takes. Its law scores 0.899 of 1 for independence, 11th of 155 countries, and no government pressure was reported in the quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case is documented: in 2023 a criminal complaint accused governor Senad Softic of suspected wrongdoing in several matters, including a project to acquire an office building in Pale and a procedure to buy land in Sarajevo. The prosecutor's office said in February 2023 that it had opened a case and was verifying the allegations, which remain unproven, while the bank said examining allegations is not an investigation and that reports of one were untrue. Grant Thornton d.o.o. Banja Luka audited the 2016 accounts. The bank holds 3.5 tonnes of gold and scores 35 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:MDA: The National Bank of Moldova issues the leu, which is held within 2 percent of the euro. Its law scores 0.861 of 1 for independence, where 1 means the bank holds the power, and it scores 30 of 100 for exposure to outside influence. Dorin Dragutanu resigned as governor on 21 September 2015 after criticism for failing to prevent about 1 billion dollars disappearing from three Moldovan banks; he blamed pressure from politicians and denied responsibility, and President Nicolae Timofti and Prime Minister Valeriu Strelet had both said he should go. On 5 March 2020 prosecutors searched the bank's headquarters and detained deputy governor Cincilei, former deputy governor Tabirta and a division head on suspicion of fraud and money laundering tied to that theft, which surfaced in 2014 and 2015 after the bank made a 13 billion leu emergency loan later turned into public debt; they also moved to arrest Dragutanu. None of it is proven. On the evening of 21 December parliament dismissed governor Octavian Armasu by 81 votes, citing insufficient and defective work on the fraud case. KPMG Moldova SRL checks the bank's accounts from outside.
p:ZMB: The Bank of Zambia issues the kwacha, which floats within a band of about 5 percent against the US dollar. Zambia scores 32 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 fully exposed, and its law scores 0.637 of 1 for written independence from government. Denny Kalyalya came to the governorship in February 2015 from the World Bank Group, where he had been executive director for the Africa Group One constituency. On 22 August 2020 President Edgar Lungu dismissed him, less than a week after he warned of economic difficulties, and appointed Christopher Mvunga from the finance ministry; Kalyalya returned as governor in October 2021. In October 2015 the Drug Enforcement Commission arrested a section officer for theft by a public servant and money laundering, accusing him of taking 43,660 US dollars and 20,335 kwacha in cash between January and September 2015; he was charged, and no court outcome is given, so the accusation is unproven. The Auditor General audits the accounts each year under the Bank of Zambia Act No. 5 of 2022.
p:MAR: Bank Al-Maghrib issues Morocco's dirham, held to a pre-announced peg, meaning a fixed rate, against the euro. It prints the notes and mints the coins at its own unit, Dar As-Sikkah, founded in 1987, and is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. Morocco scores 26 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and no government pressure was reported between 2010 and 2018. Two cases are on record, both under investigation and unproven. In 2022 the bank complained to the prosecutor's office about one of its own staff and a service provider over suspected corruption in awarding contracts, with no amounts, charges or ruling given. On 4 July 2019 it said 1.2 million dirhams, about 125,000 US dollars, had been stolen while cash was moved from the Dar As-Sikkah mint to northern cities, and opened an investigation, with no findings reported. Abdellatif Jouahri was named wali, or governor, in 2003, coming from the presidency of the CIMR, a private-sector employers' pension body.
p:LAO: The Bank of the Lao P.D.R. is the central bank of Laos, which uses the kip; its top-denomination 100,000-kip note is printed by Goznak, the Russian state currency works. One case is recorded and it ended in convictions. On 8 September 2026 the Vientiane People's Court sentenced two former directors general to life imprisonment for abusing their positions to withdraw foreign currency from the bank's reserves and exchange unlimited amounts; one of them, Aod, was sentenced in his absence because he died during the proceedings. In a related case nine bank employees were convicted of corruption and money laundering, including trading currency at special rates. Losses across the cases exceeded 2.29 trillion kip, about 102.6 million US dollars. Government pressure was reported in 1 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, and that instance was a demand to print money. The bank has two swap lines with China, arrangements to borrow each other's currency: one of 6 billion yuan, and one from January 2020 with no amount stated. Laos scores 37 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:TON: The National Reserve Bank of Tonga issues the pa'anga (TOP), which follows a crawling peg or a band of 1% or less against the US dollar. It scores 5.5 of 15 on what it tells the public. On the map's scale, 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed; Tonga scores 31. Two cases are documented. In 2024-2025 Tonga's Anti-Corruption Commissioner sued the bank and its directors, alleging that a 2024 staff payment (for example $6,600 to each of 73 staff) was an unlawful bonus linked to record profit; the board had described it as a one-off anniversary payout, and on 20 November 2025 the Court of Appeal dismissed the proceeding. In 2017-2019 a Senior Exchange Control Officer forged a Government bond to support another person's New Zealand visa application and asked for $2,500 pa'anga. She pleaded guilty and her employment was terminated; the Supreme Court of Tonga ruled on 21 May 2019. The bank's accounts for the year to 30 June 1993, published in the Tonga Government Gazette, carry an auditor's report signed by Coopers & Lybrand at Suva, Fiji, on 21 September 1993. De La Rue printed the 100-pa'anga note in the family introduced on 4 December 2023.
p:ALB: The Bank of Albania is Albania's central bank and issues the lek, kept close to the euro without any formal promise to do so; it scores 23 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. In July 2014 one of its employees was found to have stolen 713 million lek, nearly seven million US dollars, from the reserves. On 5 September 2014 prosecutors arrested governor Fullani and the bank's senior auditor and charged them with abuse of office over alleged mismanagement linked to that theft; the board dismissed Fullani, and the charges remain unproven, with no verdict reported. No government pressure was reported in 37 quarters to 2018. The bank signed a swap line with China for 2 billion yuan on 3 April 2018, letting the two central banks lend each other their currencies; a borrowing line with the European Central Bank expired on 15 January 2024.
p:KAZ: The National Bank of Kazakhstan issues the tenge, which floats within a de facto band of about 5 per cent against the US dollar, and gold makes up 77 per cent of its reserves, 368.4 tonnes. On 2 November 2015 President Nursultan Nazarbayev replaced chairman Kayrat Kelimbetov with presidential adviser Daniyar Akishev, telling parliament that confidence in the bank and the tenge had fallen and that tenge liquidity was short; Kelimbetov is not quoted. It prints its own money through the Banknote Factory of the National Bank, one of its subsidiaries, which also makes passports, identity and payment cards and has released three series of tenge notes. Landqart AG says the bank's 20,000 tenge note, issued for the 30th anniversary of independence, is printed on its Durasafe material, the second such note the bank has issued. PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP audited the accounts for the year ended 31 December 2025. It has five swap lines, arrangements to borrow another central bank's currency: Turkiye for 28.0 billion Turkish lira in 2025, Russia for 35 billion roubles on 28 May 2026 and China for 7 billion yuan on 14 December 2014. Kazakhstan scores 27 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:TGO: Togo uses the West African CFA franc, issued by the Central Bank of West African States, the BCEAO, which sets monetary policy for eight member countries. The currency is fixed at one euro to 655.957 CFA francs, and France guarantees it by lending to the BCEAO if its foreign exchange reserves run out; an agreement signed on 21 December 2019 replaced the 1973 one and ended the rule that at least half those reserves sit at the French Treasury. One case is recorded: a summit of UEMOA heads of state accepted governor Dacoury-Tabley's resignation in January 2011, after he was criticized for ignoring a 23 December decision by UEMOA finance ministers that gave Alassane Ouattara power over the institution, and the article says the BCEAO paid 60 to 100 billion CFA francs to the Gbagbo regime afterwards. Togo scores 40 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:CZE: The Czech National Bank issues the koruna and scores 18 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, leaving it less exposed than 97 percent of the places measured. It is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, the bank used by central banks themselves. Ales Michl was an economist and investment strategist at Raiffeisenbank from 2006 to 2015 and an external economic adviser to the finance ministry from 2014 to 2018 and later to Prime Minister Andrej Babis, joined the bank's board in December 2018 and was then appointed governor in succession to Jiri Rusnok. Czech Television reports that he founded Michl Fund Management in 2016, which co-founded the qualified-investor fund Robot Asset Management SICAV, that he later placed the company in a trust, and that some experts believe he may still have influence over it, which he denies; no ethics finding is recorded. In 2026 police arrested a long-serving employee accused of misappropriating tens of millions of koruna, after suspicious transactions on his account were flagged; the bank confirmed the theft was being investigated at its Brno branch, and the accusation is unproven. Government pressure was reported in 3 of the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, all of it pressing for tighter policy, alongside three threats to replace leaders. State Street Global Advisors has held an equity mandate from the bank since 2007, since raised to 7.5 billion US dollars, and also advises it on alternatives to its reserve strategies; BNP Paribas Asset Management agreed a 500 million dollar mortgage-backed securities mandate in November 2019; and Ernst & Young Audit, s.r.o. audits the accounts. Some of the gold is kept in the bank's own high-security vault in Prague, mostly for making its gold coins, with most of the reserve stored in London under no named institution, which is storage rather than management. A commemorative banknote marking the establishment of the Czechoslovak currency, which entered circulation on 30 March 2022, carries the imprint of Statni tiskarna cenin; who prints the circulating notes is not stated.
p:ETH: The National Bank of Ethiopia issues the birr. It scores 32 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, more exposed than 61% of the 194 places scored. Its legal independence is low: 0.495 of 1 on one index of 42 rules and 0.291 of 1 on another, rank 176 of 191. Government pressure was reported in 3 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, mostly pressing to cut rates or ease. One case is recorded. In March 2008 Ethiopian anti-corruption officials arrested 26 people after 90 kilos of fake gold were found in the bank's vaults: 7 from the bank, 4 from the Ethiopian Geological Survey and 15 businessmen and collaborators. What is known covers the arrests only, not charges or court outcomes. Some of the notes are made abroad: the bank awarded Francois-Charles Oberthur Fiduciaire of France a 19.6 million birr share of a 206 million birr banknote printing deal, covering the 50 birr note.
p:GBR: The Bank of England is the central bank of the United Kingdom and issues the pound sterling. It scores 21 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, 181st of the 194 places with a figure, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it. Two cases are recorded. Deputy governor Charlotte Hogg resigned on 14 March 2017 after the House of Commons Treasury Committee called it a very serious breach that she had repeatedly failed, since joining the Bank in 2013, to declare that her brother was director of group strategy at the bank Barclays; she said she had also unintentionally misled the committee. The Bank itself passed material on its 2007 and 2008 liquidity auctions to the Serious Fraud Office, which investigated from 2015 and closed the matter in June 2017, finding no evidence of criminality. Eighteen career moves between the Bank and private finance are on file. Mervyn King joined Citigroup as a senior adviser after retiring as governor in 2013, and Katharine Braddick moves from Barclays to deputy governor for prudential regulation on 1 July 2026, barred for six months from decisions on Barclays.
p:USA: The US dollar is issued through the Federal Reserve System. Banks that join hold stock in their district's Reserve Bank, and at the end of 2018 Citibank held 42.8 per cent of the New York Fed and JPMorgan Chase 29.5 per cent; member banks elect six of each Reserve Bank's nine directors, though the Board says the System is not owned by anyone. It scores 54 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, more than 98 per cent of the 194 places with a figure, and its weakest side is influence from inside. Many moves between the Fed and private finance are recorded, and none is an accusation: Alfred Hayes came to the New York Fed presidency from the New York Trust Company in 1956 and became chairman of Morgan Stanley International in November 1975; Allan Sproul left that presidency in 1956 for a Wells Fargo Bank directorship; Timothy Geithner was made president of the private equity firm Warburg Pincus in November 2013; Brian Sack ran the New York Fed's Markets Group until 2012 and joined the hedge fund manager the D. E. Shaw group; Loretta Mester joined the board of the reinsurer RenaissanceRe Holdings in November 2024; and Alberto Musalem became St. Louis Fed president in April 2024, having worked at Tudor Investment Corporation, the New York Fed and Evince Asset Management. Janet Yellen's disclosures show more than 7 million dollars of speaking income, including 952,200 dollars from Citigroup. On trading by officials, the Fed's Inspector General found in September 2024 that trades made for Raphael Bostic from 2017 broke ethics rules but no insider trading law; in January 2024 that Robert Kaplan's 2020 trades looked like acting on confidential policy information, with Eric Rosengren having failed to report his; and on 15 November 2025 that Adriana Kugler's 2024 trades broke Fed rules. Jerome Powell's and Richard Clarida's trades were cleared, and Jeffrey Lacker resigned in April 2017 over a 2012 leak, without charges. President Donald Trump has said Powell should resign, the Justice Department subpoenaed the Fed in January 2026, and after he moved to fire Governor Lisa Cook the Supreme Court ruled on 29 June 2026 that she stays.
p:VUT: Vanuatu's money, the vatu, is issued by the Reserve Bank of Vanuatu, created in 1980 and held within a band of 2 percent or less against the Australian dollar. The country scores 33 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around the bank; independence written into its law scores 0.498 of 1. One case is on record. An Ombudsman report of 3 July 1996 found that governor Samson Ngwele improperly signed ten bank guarantees worth 100 million US dollars in total, without the board's approval and under pressure from Finance Minister Barak Sope, breaching the Reserve Bank Act and the Leadership Code. The guarantees went to Peter Harold Swanson for a trading programme the Ombudsman called a scam, and were still in circulation when the report was written. The report commended Ngwele's later attempts to put things right; he disagreed with its adverse comments about him. Note Printing Australia's customer list says it has produced and supplied polymer banknotes to the bank, without a date or contract value, and the 2019 accounts were audited by KPMG, a Fiji partnership.
p:JAM: The Bank of Jamaica issues the Jamaican dollar and moves its rate against the US dollar in small announced steps. It scores 26 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and no government pressure was reported in the 37 quarters to 2018. One case is recorded and unproven: governor Derick Latibeaudiere borrowed 51 million dollars from the bank for a house, furnishings and landscaping. At a Public Accounts Committee hearing on 26 May 2009, Auditor General Pamela Monroe Ellis said she had no documents showing the loans were secured and that 25 million of it was still unsecured; the bank's lawyer said 30 million was fully secured against the governor's house, and the committee told both sides to resolve their differences and report back. Richard Byles became governor on 19 August 2019, after running Pan Caribbean Merchant Bank from 1988, the Pan Jam group from 1991 for thirteen years and Sagicor Jamaica from 2004 until he retired in 2017. Crown Agents Investment Management manages the bank's investments of special drawing rights, which began at 250 million US dollars and have since doubled, with the bank leaving the investment decisions to the firm. De La Rue prints the banknotes. The Independent Auditor's Report in the bank's Annual Report 2025 is issued by Ernst & Young Chartered Accountants of Kingston and signed on 4 March 2026.
p:DZA: The Bank of Algeria issues the dinar and holds it within a band of 2 per cent or less against the euro. Algeria scores 41 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, more exposed than 83 per cent of the 194 places with a figure, its weakest side corruption and secrecy around the bank. Government pressure was reported in 3 of the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, every time a demand to print money. One case is recorded, and it ended in acquittal: in the Khalifa Bank case the Blida criminal court sentenced former governor Abdelwahab Keramane in absentia to 20 years in prison in 2007, and on 7 June 2022 the same court acquitted him. The bank holds 173.6 tonnes of gold and is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements.
p:RWA: The National Bank of Rwanda issues the Rwandan franc, which in practice follows a crawling peg against the US dollar, meaning the rate is allowed to drift slowly in a managed way. It scores 27 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, and no government pressure was reported in the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case is recorded: the bank lost 63 million Rwandan francs from deposit accounts in early 2014 in a fraud reported to involve its own staff. Its director for information technology said the suspects had manipulated the bank's internal security system before taking the cash. One person was arrested and the file went to the Prosecutor General, while police said the main suspect was believed to have fled to Uganda; the matter is under investigation, so nothing in it is proven. De La Rue printed the 2,000-franc note introduced on 3 September 2024.
p:CUW: The Central Bank of Curaçao and Sint Maarten issues the Caribbean guilder (XCG), pegged to the US dollar. It scores 50 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, more exposed than 96% of the 194 places scored. Neither independence index codes it. Crane Currency, headquartered in Massachusetts, was contracted to print the new banknotes. One case is recorded. In July 2024 a court found former president Tromp and former deputy director Laurents guilty of document forgery over a backdated 2009 loan agreement under which over $400,000 went to Tromp's pension account. It acquitted them of official bribery and money laundering, including over a $1.5 million 2015 payment from the Venezuelan company Enpiso.
p:BRN: Brunei Darussalam Central Bank issues the Brunei dollar and runs it as a currency board, meaning the dollar is held at a fixed rate against the Singapore dollar. Under an agreement set up in 1967, the Brunei bank and Singapore's monetary authority each take in the other's notes and coins from banks and exchange them at par without charge. The bank has one swap line, an arrangement to borrow another central bank's currency, through the ASEAN+3 regional scheme, to which Brunei contributes 0.06 billion US dollars against a maximum arrangement of 0.3 billion, though the factsheet says the member is the country, not necessarily the central bank. Note Printing Australia has printed notes for Brunei: the Reserve Bank of Australia's 2007 report lists the Brunei Currency and Monetary Board among that printer's export orders in 2006/07, without giving a number of notes. PricewaterhouseCoopers Services audits the accounts. No case at the bank is documented. Its law scores 0.704 of 1 for independence from government, and it scores 46 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:SAU: Saudi Arabia's money is the riyal, issued by the Saudi Central Bank and held at a fixed rate against the United States dollar. It scores 28 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. The independence the law gives it is thinner: 0.501 of 1 on an index of 42 rules, rank 138 of 155, where 1 would mean the bank rather than the government holds the power, and 0 on the part covering control of its own money and budget. It tells the public little, 5.5 of 15 on a transparency measure, and no case at the bank is documented, which is not proof that none happened. The bank part-owns the Bank for International Settlements, the bank for central banks in Basel; its officials also sit on the Financial Stability Board, and it holds 323.1 tonnes of gold. It has one swap line, an arrangement to borrow another central bank's currency, signed with China on 20 November 2023 for three years and worth 50 billion yuan or 26 billion riyals. Governor Fahad Al-Mubarak came from private finance: general manager of Rana Investment Company from 1992 to 1999, then chairman and managing director of Morgan Stanley Saudi Arabia. He was governor from 2011 to 2016, and King Salman named him governor again by royal decree on 24 January 2021; no ethics finding is recorded against him. Banknotes are reported to be printed at home by the Saudi Central Bank Printing Works. PricewaterhouseCoopers and Ernst & Young Professional Services audited the accounts for the year ended 30 June 2023.
p:LCA: St. Lucia has no central bank of its own: it uses the EC dollar, issued by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank for eight members, among them Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada and Saint Lucia. The currency has been fixed at EC$2.70 to one US dollar since July 1976, and the law requires reserves of at least 60 per cent of currency in circulation; the agreement was signed on 5 July 1983. One case is recorded. After the bank seized the Stanford-owned Bank of Antigua, the Official Stanford Investors Committee sued it in Dallas in 2013, alleging it fraudulently misappropriated assets belonging to Stanford's victims and creditors. On 17 August 2018 a US federal judge dismissed the claims in full because the bank and Antigua are immune under US foreign sovereign immunity law, without ruling on whether the allegations were true. For St. Lucia the arrangement scores 26 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:DMA: Dominica's money is the East Caribbean dollar, issued by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank, which sets monetary policy for eight members: Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, Montserrat, St Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. The rate has been fixed at EC$2.70 to one US dollar since July 1976, when the peg moved from sterling, and the founding agreement of 5 July 1983 requires reserves of at least 60 per cent of currency in circulation and other demand liabilities. One case is recorded, and it was dismissed. After the bank seized the Stanford-owned Bank of Antigua, the Official Stanford Investors Committee sued it in Dallas in 2013, alleging it had fraudulently misappropriated assets belonging to Stanford's victims and creditors. On 17 August 2018 a United States federal judge dismissed the claims in full because the bank and Antigua are immune under US foreign sovereign immunity law, without ruling on whether the allegations were true. No government pressure was reported in any of the 37 quarters surveyed from 2010 to 2018. De La Rue supplies the polymer the notes are made of and, by one report on the updated family announced on 9 July 2026, prints them; PricewaterhouseCoopers Eastern Caribbean audits the accounts. Dominica scores 25 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, less than 83 per cent of the 194 places scored.
p:VCT: St Vincent and the Grenadines shares the East Caribbean dollar with seven other places, all served by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank, set up under an agreement signed on 5 July 1983. The rate has been fixed at 2.70 East Caribbean dollars to one US dollar since July 1976, and the law requires reserves worth at least 60 per cent of the currency in circulation. The bank's legal independence is 0.549 of 1 on an index of 42 rules, where 1 means the bank rather than the government holds the power, and government pressure was reported in none of the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case is recorded. After the bank seized the Stanford-owned Bank of Antigua, the Official Stanford Investors Committee sued it in Dallas in 2013, alleging it misappropriated assets belonging to Stanford's victims and creditors; on 17 August 2018 a US federal judge dismissed the claims in full because the bank and Antigua are immune under US foreign sovereign immunity law, and did not decide whether the allegations were true. The score for St Vincent and the Grenadines is 25 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence; the weakest part is corruption and secrecy around it, mainly laws that hide who owns money and money-laundering risk in its banks.
p:GRD: Grenada's money is the EC dollar, issued not by a national bank but by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank for eight members, among them Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada and Saint Lucia. The agreement was signed on 5 July 1983. The currency has been fixed at EC$2.70 to US$1.00 since July 1976, when the peg moved from sterling to the US dollar, and the law requires reserves of at least 60 per cent of currency in circulation. For Grenada the bank scores 26 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, and its legal independence is 0.549 of 1 on Romelli's rules; no government pressure was reported in 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. One case is recorded and it was dismissed: after the bank seized the Stanford-owned Bank of Antigua, the Official Stanford Investors Committee sued it in Dallas in 2013, alleging it had fraudulently taken assets belonging to Stanford's victims and creditors; on 17 August 2018 a United States federal judge dismissed the claims in full because the bank and Antigua are immune under US foreign sovereign immunity law, without ruling on whether the allegations were true. De La Rue supplies the polymer the notes are printed on and printed the 2027 family; PricewaterhouseCoopers Eastern Caribbean audits the accounts.
p:SYR: The Central Bank of Syria issues the Syrian pound, which moves within a band of about 5 percent against the US dollar. Government pressure was reported in 11 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, each time pressing the bank to ease and demanding that it print money. One case runs from 2005 to 2011: a Vienna court found that the Austrian banknote printer OeBS had overcharged the bank by 14 percent on banknote contracts and that the kickback returned to local decision makers. Prosecutors had told the court that former OeBS employees paid bribes to officials at Syrian and Azerbaijani banks in exchange for contracts to print money, an allegation as reported. OeBS managers were convicted in 2014 and again on retrial in 2018, and no Syrian official was named or tried in those proceedings. A circulating 500-pound note, part of the series that dropped two zeros from the pound, is printed by Goznak, the Russian state currency works. Syria scores 38 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and 15 of 100 on the Corruption Perceptions Index.
p:TJK: The National Bank of Tajikistan issues the somoni, which it keeps within a band of 2 per cent or less against the US dollar. One case is recorded, as an official finding: in March 2008 the International Monetary Fund's Executive Board found the bank had supplied inaccurate information on the cotton sector, international reserves, net domestic assets and credit policy, reporting reserves of about 450 million US dollars when they were roughly a third of that and concealing that reserves were pledged as collateral for cotton loans; Tajikistan was required to repay 47.4 million US dollars. No government pressure was reported from 2010 to 2018. It has one swap line, an arrangement to borrow another central bank's currency: 3 billion yuan with China, signed on 3 September 2015 to run three years and extendable by agreement, drawn on for 1 million yuan in January 2016; whether it is in force is not known. Its commemorative 100-somoni note, circulated on 30 October 2025, was printed by Giesecke+Devrient of Germany, that note alone and not the regular series.
p:ATG: Antigua and Barbuda uses the East Caribbean dollar, issued by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank, which sets monetary policy for eight members, among them Anguilla, Dominica, Grenada, Montserrat and Saint Lucia. The currency has been fixed at 2.70 East Caribbean dollars to one US dollar since July 1976, and the law requires an external reserve worth at least 60 per cent of the currency in circulation and other demand liabilities. Its laws score 0.549 of 1 on one measure of independence and 0.642 on another, where 1 means the bank rather than the government holds the power; the rules on lending to government score 0.08 on the first. Government pressure was reported in none of the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. In one case the Official Stanford Investors Committee sued the bank in Dallas in 2013, alleging it fraudulently misappropriated assets after it seized the Stanford-owned Bank of Antigua; on 17 August 2018 a US federal judge dismissed the claims in full because the bank and Antigua are immune under US foreign sovereign immunity law, and the court did not rule on whether the allegations were true. The exposure score is 27 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence; the highest part is corruption and secrecy around it, at 53. De La Rue prints the notes and PricewaterhouseCoopers Eastern Caribbean audits the accounts.
p:AIA: Anguilla has no central bank of its own: it uses the EC dollar, issued by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank, the monetary authority for eight places, Anguilla, Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, Montserrat, St Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, and St Vincent and the Grenadines. The currency has been fixed at EC$2.70 to one US dollar since July 1976, when the peg moved from sterling, backed by a legal requirement to hold reserves of at least 60 per cent of currency in circulation. One case is recorded. The Official Stanford Investors Committee sued the bank in Dallas in 2013 after it seized the Stanford-owned Bank of Antigua, alleging it fraudulently misappropriated assets belonging to Stanford's victims and creditors. On 17 August 2018 a US federal judge dismissed the claims in full because the bank and Antigua are immune under US foreign sovereign immunity law, and did not rule on whether the allegations were true. For Anguilla the arrangement scores 27 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:MSR: Montserrat uses the East Caribbean dollar, issued by the Eastern Caribbean Central Bank, which sets monetary policy for eight members, among them Montserrat, Anguilla, Dominica and Saint Lucia. The rate has been fixed at EC$2.70 to one US dollar since July 1976, and the founding agreement of 5 July 1983 requires reserves of at least 60 per cent of currency in circulation and other demand liabilities. One case is recorded and it was dismissed: after the bank seized the Stanford-owned Bank of Antigua, the Official Stanford Investors Committee sued it in Dallas in 2013, alleging it had fraudulently misappropriated assets belonging to Stanford's victims and creditors, and on 17 August 2018 a United States federal judge dismissed the claims in full because the bank and Antigua are immune under US foreign sovereign immunity law, without ruling on whether the allegations were true. No government pressure was reported in any of the 37 quarters surveyed from 2010 to 2018. De La Rue supplies the polymer the notes are made of and, by one report, prints them under what governor Timothy Antoine called a long-term service agreement, with no value given; PricewaterhouseCoopers Eastern Caribbean audits the accounts. Montserrat scores 32 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, pulled up by corruption and secrecy around it, at 71, mainly because local law hides who owns money.
p:BTN: Bhutan's central bank is the Royal Monetary Authority, which issues the ngultrum and keeps it pegged, or fixed, to the Indian rupee; the rupee circulates in the country as well. An anonymous informer raised a case in October 2014, and the final findings of Bhutan's Anti-Corruption Commission, covering 2014 to 2016, said a former deputy governor had allegedly forged official documents, misused power and concealed earnings from World Bank and Asian Development Bank projects. Those allegations are unproven; the case was forwarded to the Office of the Attorney General, with no later outcome. A currency swap with India, letting each side borrow up to 100 million US dollars, was signed on 17 March 2016 and ran out in March 2019. A commemorative 1,000-ngultrum note marking the Fourth King's seventieth birth anniversary was printed by De La Rue, not the ordinary circulating series, and the accounts for 2003 and 2004 were audited by M/s P.K. Mitra & Company. The bank scores 25 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:XKX: Kosovo has no currency of its own and uses the euro; its central bank is the Central Bank of the Republic of Kosovo. It used the Deutsche Mark from September 1999 and changed to the euro in 2002, the changeover finishing on 28 February 2002 in cooperation with the ECB. No exposure score is given, because too little data exists. In July 2010 European Union law enforcement officials arrested governor Hashim Rexhepi on suspicion of abuse of position, bribery, tax evasion, trading in influence and money laundering. A judge of the EU mission Eulex threw out all the charges on December 12, and in January 2012 Eulex said its prosecutor would take no further action after losing an appeal; he was acquitted. The bank has also joined the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, or RAMP. It describes that membership as building its own capacity in asset management, risk management and financial reporting rather than a handover of reserves; the World Bank, announcing an agreement signed on 16 April 2026 by Jorge Familiar and Governor Ahmet Ismaili, says a portion of the reserves will be managed from 2026.
p:PNG: The Bank of Papua New Guinea issues the kina, whose rate against the US dollar is shifted in small steps rather than left to the market, and the country scores 36 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. One case is on record. Court documents obtained by the journalism group OCCRP show that the National Fraud and Anti-Corruption Directorate searched the bank's offices in August and September 2023 in a money-laundering investigation into Genia, then acting governor; she won a temporary halt that was later dismissed, she has not been charged, and it remains under investigation and unproven. She had earlier been under fraud-squad investigation over a firearms deal for the bank's security team, and became governor in early 2024. In April 2024 the Prime Minister announced new board members, among them Sir Robin Fleming, former chief executive of the commercial bank Bank South Pacific, and Mark Baker, former country head of the commercial bank Australia and New Zealand Banking. The 2024 annual report names Pictet Asset Management as the weakest of the outside firms running part of the reserves that year, with DWS and BlackRock the strongest. Note Printing Australia listed the bank among its export orders in 2006 and 2007.
p:MKD: North Macedonia's money is the denar, issued by the National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia and held in practice at a fixed rate to the euro. It scores 24 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it. One case is recorded, running from 2017 to 2020, and it is unproven: an association of depositors of Eurostandard Bank said in a press release that the governor tipped off the finance minister and other large depositors so they could take their money out before the bank was put under administration, and that financial police reports were kept secret so it could keep operating. The association said Finance Minister Nina Angelovska withdrew more than 200,000 euros months before the central bank acted, and that over 60 million euros were lost; no charges and no official finding are reported. The European Central Bank gave the bank a temporary line to borrow euros against collateral from 15 December 2022 to 15 January 2024, which has expired.
p:BLZ: The Central Bank of Belize issues the Belize dollar, held at a fixed rate to the US dollar. In August 2021 governor Gustavo Manuel Vasquez lost his post. Prime Minister John Briceno said the board had recommended he resign because of a lot of policy differences. Vasquez wrote that his appointment was terminated on the instructions of the Ministry of Finance, that he faced opposition from it, and that he had tried to restore the bank's integrity and operational autonomy. Castillo Sanchez & Burrell, LLP, Chartered Accountants audited the 2013 accounts, and De La Rue printed the new 100-dollar note introduced on 4 August 2025. Belize scores 32 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and it tells the public little, 4 of 15 on a transparency measure in 2019.
p:GIN: Guinea's money, the Guinean franc, is issued by the Central Bank of the Republic of Guinea. The country scores 30 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and the weakest part is corruption and secrecy around the bank. In December 2021 the country's military leader, Mamadi Doumbouya, dismissed Laounceny Kaba, who had run the bank for ten years, along with the two vice-governors, Baidy Aribot and Madjou Sow, and a younger economist, Karamo Kaba, replaced him; the report of 8 December 2021 puts the removal down to how long Kaba had held the post and to his closeness to the deposed president, Alpha Condé, and says, as a report rather than a confirmed fact, that he had tried without success to win the junta's confidence. On 23 June 2026 the appeals chamber of Guinea's CRIEF court convicted a former governor, Bah, in his absence of embezzlement of public funds and related offences, sentencing him to five years, ordering him to repay 10.5 million US dollars taken from the bank's coffers without trace, imposing a fine of 5 billion Guinean francs and confiscating assets; his defence said the money was released on the instruction of the highest state authorities. Government pressure was reported in 4 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, each time to loosen policy and to print money.
p:COM: The Central Bank of the Comoros issues the Comorian franc, and France stands behind it. A monetary cooperation agreement signed at Moroni and Paris on 23 November 1979 rests on an unlimited French guarantee of the currency the bank issues. That agreement set the rate at 1 Comorian franc to 0.02 French francs; after a devaluation of 33 percent on 11 January 1994, the rate is now 1 euro to 491.968 Comorian francs. The bank must keep 65 percent of its foreign currency reserves on deposit with the French Treasury. Under statutes in force since March 2025, France names two of the six board members, two of the four members of the banking supervision committee and two of the four members of the committee that sets monetary policy and manages reserves. The notes are printed by the Banque de France, the French central bank; a new 10,000-franc note was reportedly introduced on 6 January 2026. Independence written into its law scores 0.439 of 1 on one index and 0.682 on another, where 1 means the bank rather than the government holds the power. No documented case at the bank was found, which does not prove none happened. It holds no gold, Mazars Fivoarana audited its 2024 accounts, and it scores 61 of 100, the highest of the 194 places with a figure.
p:TKM: The Central Bank of Turkmenistan issues the manat. Its law leaves most of the power with the government: 0.41 of 1 on one independence index, where 1 means the bank holds the power, and 0.183 on another, ranking it 187 of 191. It scores 33 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, the largest part being corruption and secrecy around it, at 74. In March 2002 the prosecutor's office accused former central bank chairman Orazov of embezzling 120 million US dollars in German and Swiss loans. On 29 December 2002 the Supreme Court sentenced Orazov in absentia to 25 years over alleged involvement in the armed attack on President Niyazov of 25 November 2002, and the People's Council raised that to life imprisonment the next day; Amnesty International called the trial grossly unfair. That conviction is for the alleged attack, not the loan accusation, which remains unproven. In January 2014 President Gurbanguly Berdymukhamedov dismissed the bank's head, Tuvakmammet Japarov, for unspecified flaws in his work.
p:MRT: The Central Bank of Mauritania issues Mauritania's money, the ouguiya, and scores 28 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed; its weakest side is corruption in the country and money-laundering risk in its banks. One case is recorded, from 2020 and 2021, and it is still an investigation. In July 2020 police working under the Nouakchott-Ouest prosecutor arrested six people, one of them a bank employee, over foreign currency taken from the central bank. Early reports put the amount at about 1 million US dollars and later reports at 2.4 million, plus 500,000 dollars in counterfeit notes. By March 2021 seven people were in pretrial detention, presumed to have taken about 1 million dollars, and supporters held a sit-in demanding a quick trial. No trial or verdict is reported. The governor also signed an agreement with the World Bank treasury for advice on managing reserves.
p:ARE: The Central Bank of the United Arab Emirates issues the dirham and holds it at a fixed rate against the US dollar, an arrangement called a peg. It scores 27 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. No case at the bank is documented, and no government pressure was reported in the 37 quarters surveyed between 2010 and 2018. Its law gives it middling independence, 0.685 of 1. It is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements. Its notes are printed by Oumolat Security Printing, which the Emirates Investment Authority started and owned before it was transferred to the central bank; a new 100 dirham polymer note printed by Oumolat was reported on 31 March 2025. Abdulhamid Saeed, made governor by federal decree on 2 April 2020, had been group chief executive of First Abu Dhabi Bank.
p:PAN: Panama has no central bank. Banco Nacional de Panamá is a state commercial bank, and the country uses the US dollar. The IMF lists Panama with Ecuador, El Salvador, the Marshall Islands, Micronesia, Palau and Timor-Leste as having no separate legal tender, with the US dollar as anchor. The US dollar is 89.08% of world currency trading, 56.7% of foreign reserves and 50.1% of Swift payments, and 16 places use it. No documented case at a central bank was found. The country has had 1 systemic banking crisis since 1970, and its financial secrecy score is 78.4 of 100. The exposure score is 53 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 fully exposed, which ranks 6 of 194; corruption and secrecy around it scores 67 and outside influence 39.
p:BDI: The Bank of the Republic of Burundi is the central bank of Burundi, which uses the Burundian franc. One case is recorded. In October 2023 the Ministry of Justice said that the dismissed governor, Dieudonné Murengerantwari, was being prosecuted for passive corruption (taking bribes), money laundering, misappropriation of public property and undermining the national economy. The prosecutor called this description of the facts provisional, and the governor was being questioned at the time of the report. He is charged, and nothing is reported as proven. The bank scores 32 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and its weakest side is corruption in the country. The bank's accounts are audited from outside the country by Forvis Mazars Cameroun SA, whose report on the year ended 30 June 2023 was signed at Bujumbura on 6 August 2026.
p:ARM: Armenia uses the dram, issued by the Central Bank of Armenia, which scores 20 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. The dram is held on a pre-announced crawling peg against the US dollar, meaning the rate is moved in small announced steps. No case at the bank is recorded, and no government pressure was reported in the 37 quarters surveyed between 2010 and 2018. The bank has rejoined the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, having been a member from 2006 to 2014; what it gets is advice, onsite expertise and staff training rather than management of its assets. It has one swap line with China, an arrangement for two central banks to lend each other currency, for 77 billion drams and one billion yuan, dated March 2015, though whether it is still in force is not known. A bank representative says Giesecke+Devrient won the printing of its third banknote series after an evaluation of all offers. KPMG Armenia LLC audits the accounts.
p:CPV: The Bank of Cape Verde issues the escudo, and the government of Portugal guarantees it under a currency cooperation agreement signed on 13 March 1998. The rate is fixed at 110.265 Cape Verdean escudos to the euro, having started at 0.55 escudos to the Portuguese escudo. The Portuguese Treasury provides a short-term credit line of 27.5 million euros, which can rise to 45 million, with drawings capped at 5 million, and Cabo Verde must transfer reserves equal to 35 per cent of what it asks for; Banco de Portugal states the facility obliges neither it nor any euro-area institution to step in. The bank has also signed a technical assistance agreement with the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, becoming its 75th member, which is advisory work rather than management of its assets, and De La Rue printed the 1,000 and 2,000 escudo notes released on 15 April 2025. Its law scores 0.518 of 1 for independence, where 1 means the bank rather than the government holds the power. No case at the bank is documented, which is not proof none happened. It scores 47 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, ranking 12 of 194, with money issued, backed or fixed from abroad the main reason.
p:BRB: The Central Bank of Barbados issues the Barbados dollar and in practice holds it at a fixed rate against the United States dollar. In 2017 Finance Minister Chris Sinckler dismissed Governor Delisle Worrell. The government's stated reason was that the board objected to his reported high-handed manner; some observers believed the reason was his refusal to keep financing the government with new money, which he had set out in a letter that January saying the government must stop taking new money from the bank to pay its bills. The Appeals Court upheld the minister's right to dismiss him. Apart from that, no government pressure was reported in the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. The bank's founding governor, Sir Courtney Blackman, had been an economist at the Wall Street bank Irving Trust Company from 1968 to 1971, led the bank from 1972 to 1987 across three terms while also serving as Barbados' alternate governor to the International Monetary Fund until March 1987, and from 1987 to 1994 worked as an international business consultant and as director general of corporations and financial institutions that the bank's own page does not name. Its five-dollar polymer note, introduced in December 2022, is printed by De La Rue. Barbados scores 28 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and the bank tells the public little, 3 of 15 on a transparency measure. The bank's accounts are audited by PricewaterhouseCoopers SRL of Bridgetown, whose report for the year ended 31 December 2025 is dated 27 March 2026.
p:SDN: The Central Bank of Sudan issues the Sudanese pound. It scores 43 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, at 85. In October 2025 Sovereignty Council head Abdel Fattah al-Burhan dismissed governor Burai Al-Siddiq Ali Ahmed after a dispute over the rules for buying and exporting gold, and appointed Amna Mirghani Hassan El Toum; deputy governor Mohamed Osman Ahmed Mohamed Khair was dismissed less than two weeks later. Government pressure was reported in 2 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, both times pressing the bank to cut rates or ease and demanding that it print money. Its law scores 0.333 of 1 on one measure of independence, ranking 172 of 191, and it scores 1.5 of 15 on how much it tells the public. Its notes are made in the country: Dabanga reported in February 2019 that Sudan's new 200-pound banknote had gone into production at the Sudanese Company for Currency Printing, a domestic press the prime minister had visited that week. No documented case at the central bank was found.
p:TTO: The Central Bank of Trinidad and Tobago issues the Trinidad and Tobago dollar and in practice holds it at a fixed rate against the US dollar. Both of its records come out of the collapse of the conglomerate CL Financial and of the Hindu Credit Union. The commission of enquiry into that collapse, set up in November 2010 under a single commissioner, Sir Anthony Colman, found the bank's powers to regulate insurers 'fundamentally deficient', tracing that to how narrowly the Insurance Act was drawn; it said the Inspector of financial institutions tried to use the limited tools then available but that Clico and CL Financial management largely ignored them, and that the collapse might have been avoided had powers in an unpassed Insurance Bill been in force by 2008. It blamed no named bank official. The enquiry sat from March 2011 to May 2013 at an estimated cost of 36.2 million dollars, including a 7 million dollar fee for Colman. At the same enquiry, on 6 December 2012, Queen's Counsel Peter Carter put it to former governor Ewart Williams that intervening in 2006 would have kept more than 10 billion Trinidad and Tobago dollars out of danger; Williams said the bank had seen early warning signs at CLICO that year but held off to avoid a run on the insurer, and intervened in 2009. That was the questioning of a witness rather than a finding, and the claim is unconfirmed. The bank is listed as a member of the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, which offers members advice, training and the management of assets without the listing saying which applies here. BDO T&T audited its accounts for 2024, De La Rue printed its 100-dollar plastic note of December 2019, and it holds 2 tonnes of gold. No government pressure was reported in any of the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, and it scores 30 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:QAT: The Qatar Central Bank issues the riyal (QAR), held at a fixed rate to the US dollar (a peg). Its law scores 0.607 of 1 on one independence index and 0.586 on another, where 1 means the bank holds the power. Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters in 2010-2018, and no documented case at the bank was found. It has 4 swap lines, which are agreements to borrow another central bank's currency. They include CNY 35 billion with China, with a renewal agreement dated 14 October 2026, and USD 15 billion equivalent in lira and riyal with Türkiye, amended in 2020, whose current status is not confirmed. It holds 116.2 tonnes of gold, 26.8% of reserves. The exposure score is 28 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 fully exposed. De La Rue printed the 22-riyal commemorative note issued for the 2022 FIFA World Cup.
p:SLV: El Salvador's central bank is the Central Reserve Bank of El Salvador, and the currency is listed as both the colon and the US dollar. The IMF's 2023 classification puts the country among places with no separate legal tender of their own, using the US dollar as their anchor; legal changes made private acceptance of Bitcoin voluntary and tax payments payable only in US dollars, listed as steps taken before an IMF loan approved on 26 February 2025. The bank's accounts are audited from outside by the Corte de Cuentas de la Republica, under a law still in force. Written independence from government scores 0.789 of 1, and no government pressure was reported in any of the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. No case at the bank is documented, which does not prove none happened. The US dollar is used in 16 places and makes up 89.08 per cent of world currency trading. El Salvador scores 37 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:HND: The Central Bank of Honduras issues the lempira, kept as of December 2025 at a set level against the US dollar and moved in small steps, an arrangement called a crawling peg. Its accounts are checked from outside by Horwath Central America, for the 2023 financial year. The 200-lempira note is printed by Crane Currency, which won private tender 11/2023 by a resolution of 14 March 2024, worth 1,284,000 US dollars at 6.42 US cents a note. One case is documented: on 3 June 2026 prosecutors charged 11 current and former employees, two of them serving managers, with 100 counts of negligent embezzlement over a scheme said to have removed public funds from the bank, and they were arrested after the court admitted the case. The charges are unproven. Honduras scores 27 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, the heaviest part being corruption and secrecy around the bank, at 67.
p:STP: The Central Bank of Sao Tome and Principe issues the dobra, which is pegged to the euro. One episode is recorded. In June 2006 the cabinet dismissed the governor, Maria do Carmo Silveira, a former prime minister, together with her team, saying it had found irregularities in the construction of the new central bank building, a project valued at 8 million US dollars. No detail of those irregularities and no investigation finding was given, so the claim is unproven, and the report does not mention corruption or fraud. A commemorative 50-dobra note marking 50 years of independence, introduced on 26 August 2026, was produced by Royal Joh. Enschede in the Netherlands; that is the commemorative note, not the circulating series. The country has had two systemic banking crises since 1970, and it scores 28 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, with its weak point the corruption and secrecy around it, chiefly money-laundering risk in its banks.
p:BHR: The Central Bank of Bahrain, created in 1973, issues the Bahraini Dinar (BHD), held at a peg to the US dollar as of December 2025. Its exposure score is 28 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed. The weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it (56): the country's laws hide who owns money, and financial secrecy scores 69 of 100. Written independence from government scores 0.515 of 1 on one index (rank 135 of 155) and 0.433 on another (rank 156 of 191). Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, and no documented case at the bank was found. A swap line, which is an agreement to borrow another central bank's currency, runs both ways with the United Arab Emirates: BHD 2 billion (AED 20 billion), signed 8 April 2026, for up to 5 years. De La Rue printed the 20-dinar note. The bank's accounts are audited by KPMG Fakhro of Manama, which signed its report on the 2023 financial statements on 10 March 2024.
p:TLS: Timor-Leste has its own central bank, the Central Bank of Timor-Leste, created in 2001, but not its own currency: it uses the United States dollar. The International Monetary Fund's 2023 classification lists it among the places with no separate legal tender and the dollar as anchor. It scores 49 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, more exposed than 94 per cent of the 194 places with a figure; the outside influence part alone scores 41. Its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, 57, with a Corruption Perceptions Index score of 44 of 100 for 2025. The independence the law gives the bank is comparatively strong, 0.777 of 1 and rank 50 of 191. No documented case at the central bank was found, which does not prove none happened. The dollar it uses dominates world finance: 16 places use it, and it accounts for 89.08 per cent of world currency trading. Ernst & Young Audit & Associados - SROC, S.A. audited the 2023 accounts.
p:GUY: The Bank of Guyana issues the Guyanese dollar, held at what is in practice a fixed rate to the US dollar as of December 2025. It scores 29 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 fully exposed, and the weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, at 56, with the country scoring 40 of 100 on the Corruption Perceptions Index. Independence written into its law scores 0.609 of 1, ranking 93 of 191, and no government pressure was reported in 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. No case at the bank is recorded, which is not proof none happened. Crane Currency is listed as having supplied banknotes, banknote paper and anti-counterfeiting features, though that comes from a client list in another body's announcement rather than a contract notice. The Auditor General audits the accounts.
p:AND: Andorra has no central bank; the Andorran Financial Authority oversees its finances, and the country uses the euro. Under its monetary agreement with the EU, Andorra may issue its own euro coins from July 2013. The IMF's 2023 classification lists Andorra and San Marino as having no separate legal tender, with the euro as anchor. Little else is scored: no overall exposure score exists, and independence and public transparency are not rated. Money-laundering risk is 3.48 of 10 (rank 171 of 177, where 1 is riskiest), and financial secrecy is 54.4 of 100. No documented case was found. The European Central Bank ran a temporary repo line, a lending arrangement, with Andorra from 15 December 2022 to 15 January 2024; it has expired.
p:UZB: The Central Bank of Uzbekistan, created in 1991, issues the country's money, held at a de facto crawling peg to the US dollar as of December 2025, meaning the rate is moved in small steps. It scores 32 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed; outside influence scores 3 and corruption and secrecy around the bank 60. Written independence from government scores 0.862 of 1 on one index and 0.604 on another. Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, and no documented case at the bank was found. Gold holdings are 431.7 tonnes, 87.5% of reserves. A swap line, an agreement to borrow another central bank's currency, with China was set at 0.7 billion renminbi in April 2011; whether it is in force is not known. The notes are made by Davlat Belgisi, a state production association that the bank lists among its own subordinate organisations, taking in the Tashkent Printing Factory, the Tashkent Paper Factory and the Tashkent Mint.
p:SWZ: The Central Bank of Eswatini, set up in 1974, issues the country's currency, fixed at par to the South African rand under the Common Monetary Area. One licensing fight runs through two findings. In 2017 the bank's evaluations team recommended rejecting Farmers Bank's application for a commercial banking licence, warning it would tarnish the integrity of the bank's licensing policy, and it was turned down late that year. Governor Majozi Sithole said a royal command required him to attend a meeting about the venture on 14 July 2017, and in May 2018 finance minister Martin Dlamini told the bank that King Mswati III had ordered an investigation into its reluctance to license it. A conditional licence followed in September 2018 after a royal command. The bank revoked it on 5 October 2020 because the source of the seed capital was unexplained; an appeal chaired by commerce minister Manqoba Khumalo ruled in December 2020 that the licence should stand, and the bank reinstated it in January 2021 while objecting to procedural improprieties. A 2022 forensic report by Kroll, commissioned by the bank, said parties outside the bank had likely intervened and instructed it to proceed, and that 89 million rand of seed capital had gone from 2019 into silver bullion the bank could not verify existed. In October 2023 the bank moved its portfolio of special drawing rights to Crown Agents Investment Management, which manages it and trains bank staff; Giesecke+Devrient of Germany printed the new 20 lilangeni note. Eswatini scores 34 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and its written independence is 0.373 of 1 on the Cukierman method, where 1 means the bank holds the power. The bank's accounts are audited by SNG Grant Thornton Chartered Accountants (Eswatini) of Mbabane, which signed its report on the statements for the year ended 31 March 2026 on 26 August 2026.
p:HTI: The Bank of the Republic of Haiti, created in 1979, issues the currency HTG, held at a de facto peg to the US dollar as of December 2025; the dollar is also listed as a currency there. Its exposure score is 49 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed; that is more exposed than 95% of 194 places. Corruption and secrecy around it scores 82, with a Corruption Perceptions Index score of 16 of 100 and money-laundering risk of 8.12 of 10 (rank 2 of 177, where 1 is riskiest). Written independence from government scores 0.366 of 1 on one index (rank 151 of 155) and 0.376 on another (rank 165 of 191). Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, and no documented case at the bank was found. The bank's accounts are audited by KPMG S.A. of France together with the Port-au-Prince firm Merove-Pierre - Cabinet d'Experts-Comptables, whose joint report on the year ended 30 September 2021 was signed on 30 June 2022.
p:CRI: The Central Bank of Costa Rica issues the country's money and, as of December 2025, keeps it within a moving band of plus or minus 2 percent against the US dollar. It scores 28 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence; outside influence alone scores 5, and the weak side is corruption and secrecy around the bank, at 52. The independence written into its law is high, 0.826 of 1 on one index. Government pressure was reported in 1 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, and that instance was a threat to change the law. No documented case at the bank was found, which does not prove none happened. Semanario Universidad reports that the bank hired BlackRock in 2017 as a co-administrator of its international reserves and that BlackRock holds 5.5 percent of them, about 352 million US dollars, the bank telling the paper that hiring outside portfolio managers is usual practice in central banking. The Contraloria General de la Republica audits the accounts under the 1995 central bank law, which is in force.
p:JOR: The Central Bank of Jordan issues the Jordanian dinar and holds it at a fixed rate against the US dollar, an arrangement called a peg. No case at the bank is documented, and no government pressure was reported in the 37 quarters surveyed between 2010 and 2018. Parliament pushed once: in September 2003 members signed a petition urging Prime Minister Ali Abulragheb to remove governor Umayya Touqan, after Touqan froze all the bank accounts of six leaders of Hamas; whether the government acted on it is not known. One leader later crossed into private banking. Mohammed Said Mohammed Shahin, a former Governor and Chairman of the bank and earlier a deputy governor, became chairman of the Islamic International Arab Bank, a commercial bank, on 31 March 2017. Jordan scores 29 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, its weakest side corruption and secrecy around the bank.
p:SLB: The Solomon Islands dollar is issued by the Central Bank of Solomon Islands, created in 1976 and holding the currency at a crawling peg to the US dollar as of December 2025, meaning the rate is moved in small steps announced in advance. The country scores 31 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and the weakest side is corruption and secrecy around the bank. The bank is near the bottom of 112 places for what it tells the public, at 3 of 15. One case is recorded: a former employee, Bobongi, was convicted on 39 counts of money laundering and two counts of larceny and embezzlement for stealing more than 1.7 million dollars in old banknotes in 2007 to 2009, while the bank was destroying them, and was sentenced to nine years. Note Printing Australia's customer list says it has produced and supplied polymer banknotes to the bank, with no date or value given. Crown Agents Investment Management manages about 95 percent of the bank's allocation of special drawing rights, a reserve asset issued by the International Monetary Fund, and the Auditor General's Office audits the accounts.
p:ABW: The Central Bank of Aruba, created in 1986, issues the Aruban florin and holds it at a peg to the US dollar as of December 2025. It scores 29 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed; the weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, with financial secrecy at 67.3 of 100. Written independence from government scores 0.446 of 1, 149th of 191, with the measures for the governor and for policy making both at 0. No documented case at the bank was found. Crane Currency, a banknote maker, is listed as having supplied Aruba's new banknotes in 2019, on a client list in another organisation's announcement rather than a contract notice. BNP Paribas Asset Management runs a fixed income mandate in US dollars for the bank and also gives it advice. Ernst & Young audits the accounts.
p:MAC: Macao's money, the pataca, is issued by the Monetary Authority of Macao, and in December 2025 it was held at a fixed rate against the United States dollar. The top note of the Bank of China Macau series, the 1,000-pataca note, is printed by Hong Kong Note Printing Limited; Macao's other note-issuing bank is BNU. No documented case at the authority was found, which does not prove none happened. Its law leaves it little independence from government: 0.271 of 1 on one index, the lowest of 155 places, with its power to refuse lending to the government scored at zero. It has two borrowing lines with China's central bank, one signed on 5 December 2025 that runs both ways for 50 billion yuan, or 57 billion patacas, with no end date, and an earlier line of 30 billion renminbi from December 2019 whose standing is not known. It scores 31 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:OMN: The Central Bank of Oman, created in 1974, issues the Omani rial and holds it at a fixed rate, a peg, to the US dollar as of December 2025. No documented case at the bank was found, and no government pressure was reported in the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. Its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, with financial secrecy at 72.4 of 100. Independence written into its law scores 0.618 of 1 on one index and 0.46 on another, the law last changed in 2000. It holds 6.7 tonnes of gold, 3.6 per cent of reserves. Oman's first polymer note, a 1-rial commemorative reported for introduction on 11 January 2026, was printed by Giesecke+Devrient; that is a commemorative, not the circulating series. Oman scores 27 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. The Independent Auditor's Report in the bank's Annual Report 2023 is signed by KPMG at Muscat on 7 May 2024.
p:SYC: The Central Bank of Seychelles, set up in 1983, issues the Seychelles rupee and, as of December 2025, holds it within a band of plus or minus 2 percent against the US dollar. It scores 26 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, below three-quarters of the places measured; its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, at 49, from laws that hide who owns money and money-laundering risk in its banks. No documented case at the bank was found, which does not prove none happened. Part of its foreign currency savings is handled by outsiders. The World Bank's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership runs a portfolio of its reserves, first funded with 100 million US dollars in 2019 and still held at the end of 2025, and during 2025 it also ran workshops and executive forums and paid for staff qualifications. Crown Agents Investment Management runs a bond portfolio split evenly between US dollars and Chinese renminbi, begun in 2014 with 25.0 million US dollars and topped up by another 25.0 million in April 2022. UBS Asset Management runs a money market fund holding part of the reserves, first funded with 10.0 million US dollars in 2017 and still held at the end of 2025, and has invited bank staff to its annual reserves seminar. A trade report says the bank's new family of banknotes was printed by the British printers De La Rue, giving no contract value, volume or term. The 2025 accounts were audited by the Auditor General of Seychelles, with the audit review carried out by Grant Thornton Audit and Accounting Limited in Abu Dhabi.
p:BHS: The Central Bank of The Bahamas issues the Bahamian dollar, which as of December 2025 is held at a fixed rate against the United States dollar. The Bahamas scores 26 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 fully exposed. Its weak point is secrecy: Bahamian law makes it hard to see who owns money there, scoring 75.4 of 100 for financial secrecy, ranked 32 of 141. No government pressure was reported in any of the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. Two career moves are recorded, neither of them an accusation. T. Baswell Donaldson, who had run the Bahamas Monetary Authority from 1968, was appointed the bank's first governor on 1 June 1974 and served until May 1980; afterwards he chaired the commercial bank Commonwealth Bank, whose ownership is not stated, as well as the Securities Commission, and was ambassador to the United States. James H. Smith was governor from 1987 to 1997 and chairs CFAL, a Nassau investment management and advisory firm that describes itself as the investment arm of Colina Holdings Ltd; he was also a senator and minister of state in the Ministry of Finance from 2002 to 2007. Giesecke+Devrient printed the bank's new 1-dollar note, introduced on 3 February 2025.
