n:People's Majlis Committee for Public F: The People's Majlis Committee for Public Finance is a committee of the Maldives parliament, based in Malé. It is tied to the Maldives Monetary Authority, the central bank. It summoned Governor Ahmed Naseer twice, and he resigned in July 2019 amid allegations of circumventing the bank's regulations. Former Financial Intelligence Unit head Abdulla Ashraf alleged that Naseer interfered in unit investigations, including one into a 22.5 million rufiyaa deposit to then-President Abdulla Yameen's account shortly before the 2018 election. Naseer denied trying to influence the unit and made counter-allegations against Ashraf. The article reports no charges or findings.
n:Abdulla Yameen Abdul Gayoom: Abdulla Yameen Abdul Gayoom was President of the Maldives. He is named in a case involving the Maldives Monetary Authority, the central bank. Governor Ahmed Naseer resigned in July 2019 amid allegations of circumventing the bank's regulations, after parliament's public finance committee summoned him twice. Former Financial Intelligence Unit head Abdulla Ashraf alleged that Naseer interfered in unit investigations, including one into a 22.5 million rufiyaa deposit to Yameen's account shortly before the 2018 election. Naseer denied trying to influence the unit and made counter-allegations against Ashraf. The article reports no charges or findings.
n:Credit Bank of Cambodia: Credit Bank of Cambodia is a bank in Cambodia. It is tied to the National Bank of Cambodia, the central bank, through a loan. The Phnom Penh Post reported that Governor Thor Peng Leath issued a 3 million dollar central bank loan on 31 May 1994 so the bank could meet minimum capital requirements. Central bank officials admitted this was "highly irregular". The paper also reported that on 8 May 1995 the bank let 145,000 dollars be withdrawn from former commerce minister Var Huot's account after its assets were frozen. Creditors and senior officials claimed preferential treatment; Var Huot said there was none. These are unconfirmed claims, and the article reports no charges or findings against central bank officials.
n:Var Huot: Var Huot is a former commerce minister of Cambodia. He is tied to the National Bank of Cambodia, the central bank, through Credit Bank of Cambodia. The Phnom Penh Post reported that on 8 May 1995 the bank let 145,000 dollars be withdrawn from his account after its assets were frozen. It also reported that Governor Thor Peng Leath had issued the bank a 3 million dollar central bank loan on 31 May 1994, which central bank officials admitted was "highly irregular". Creditors and senior officials claimed preferential treatment; Var Huot said there was none. These are unconfirmed claims, and the article reports no charges or findings against central bank officials.
n:Marleau Lemire: Marleau Lemire is a company based in Canada. It is named in a case involving the National Bank of Cambodia, the central bank. The Phnom Penh Post reported that Governor Thor Peng Leath issued a 3 million dollar central bank loan on 31 May 1994 so Credit Bank of Cambodia could meet minimum capital requirements, which central bank officials admitted was "highly irregular". It also reported that on 8 May 1995 the bank let 145,000 dollars be withdrawn from former commerce minister Var Huot's account after its assets were frozen. Var Huot said there was no preferential treatment. These are unconfirmed claims, and the article reports no charges or findings against central bank officials.
n:State Comptroller of Israel: The State Comptroller of Israel is the national auditor, based in Jerusalem. It is tied to the Bank of Israel, the central bank, through two reports. A report by Comptroller Eliezer Goldberg, published on 29 April 2002, said former governor Jacob Frenkel unlawfully received hundreds of thousands of shekels when he resigned. It said he demanded and received refunds and payments his predecessors did not get, approved by a senior bank official who reported to him. Goldberg did not say whether the state should demand the money back. On 3 February 2009 Globes reported that a draft report by Comptroller Micha Lindenstrauss found alleged flaws in the bank's supervision of sub-prime investments at Bank Hapoalim. The bank said it had responses to all the points.
n:Bank Hapoalim: Bank Hapoalim is a bank based in Tel Aviv, Israel. It is named in a case involving the Bank of Israel, the central bank. Globes reported on 3 February 2009, citing sources, that a draft report by State Comptroller Micha Lindenstrauss found alleged flaws in how the central bank's supervision department handled sub-prime investments at Hapoalim. Hapoalim had written off 1.5 billion dollars on them. The report also said the central bank had only partial information about Israeli banks' exposure to risky instruments. This was a draft, and the central bank was preparing its reply, saying it had responses to all the points.
n:Auditor General's Department of Jamaic: The Auditor General's Department is Jamaica's public auditor, based in Kingston. It is tied to the Bank of Jamaica, the central bank. Governor Derick Latibeaudiere borrowed 51 million dollars from the bank for a house, furnishings and landscaping. At a Public Accounts Committee hearing on 26 May 2009, Auditor General Pamela Monroe Ellis said she had no documents showing the loans were secured and that a 25 million dollar part was still unsecured. The bank's lawyer said 30 million dollars was fully secured against the governor's house. The committee told both sides to resolve their differences and report back.
n:Public Accounts Committee of Jamaica's: The Public Accounts Committee is a committee of Jamaica's Parliament that reviews public spending, based in Kingston. It is tied to the Bank of Jamaica, the central bank. Governor Derick Latibeaudiere borrowed 51 million dollars from the bank for a house, furnishings and landscaping. At a committee hearing on 26 May 2009, Auditor General Pamela Monroe Ellis said she had no documents showing the loans were secured and that a 25 million dollar part was still unsecured. The bank's lawyer said 30 million dollars was fully secured against the governor's house. The committee told both sides to resolve their differences and report back.
n:Sandro Gozi: Sandro Gozi is a person tied to the Central Bank of the Republic of San Marino through a payment. Investigators suspected a 220,000 euro payment from the central bank to him was for a consultancy they considered fictitious. The case against Gozi and bank president Catia Tomasetti became public in April 2019. The Tribunal of San Marino dismissed it in 2020, finding no relevant conduct by either suspect. The article reports that the consultancy was real.
n:Tribunal of San Marino: The Tribunal of San Marino is the country's court. It is tied to the Central Bank of the Republic of San Marino through one case. Investigators suspected a 220,000 euro payment from the central bank to Sandro Gozi was for a consultancy they considered fictitious. The case against Gozi and bank president Catia Tomasetti became public in April 2019. The Tribunal dismissed it in 2020, finding no relevant conduct by either suspect. The article reports that the consultancy was real.
n:Trade Line Namibia: Trade Line Namibia is a company in Namibia that was given an exclusive prospecting licence on the Skeleton Coast. It is named in a case involving the Bank of Namibia, the central bank. Court papers in a suit brought by Nambib Resources against the Minister of Mines listed the bank's governor, Tom Alweendo, as a 10 per cent shareholder in Trade Line Namibia. Alweendo said he was made a director of the company without his knowledge. The article reports no finding or outcome.
n:Nambib Resources: Nambib Resources is a company based in Windhoek, Namibia. It is named in a case involving the Bank of Namibia, the central bank. Nambib Resources brought a suit against the Minister of Mines over an exclusive prospecting licence on the Skeleton Coast given to Trade Line Namibia. Court papers in the suit listed the bank's governor, Tom Alweendo, as a 10 per cent shareholder in Trade Line Namibia. Alweendo said he was made a director of the company without his knowledge. The article reports no finding or outcome.
n:Hawks (South African Police Service): The Hawks are the South African Police Service's unit for serious crimes. They are tied to the Central Bank of Lesotho through a fraud case. In February 2024 three South Africans appeared in the Ficksburg Magistrates Court on fraud and money laundering charges over 57 million rand allegedly stolen from the central bank. The Hawks said Lesotho officials intercepted vouchers meant for service providers and diverted the payments to co-conspirators in South Africa. They also said some officials were already before court in Lesotho. The charges are allegations, and no outcome is reported.
n:Financial Intelligence Centre: The Financial Intelligence Centre is an agency tied to the Central Bank of Lesotho through a fraud case. In February 2024 three South Africans appeared in the Ficksburg Magistrates Court on fraud and money laundering charges over 57 million rand allegedly stolen from the central bank. The Hawks, a South African police unit, said Lesotho officials intercepted vouchers meant for service providers and diverted the payments to co-conspirators in South Africa. They also said some officials were already before court in Lesotho. The charges are allegations, and no outcome is reported.
n:Ficksburg Magistrates Court: The Ficksburg Magistrates Court is a court in Ficksburg, South Africa. It is named in a case involving the Central Bank of Lesotho. In February 2024 three South Africans appeared before it on fraud and money laundering charges over 57 million rand allegedly stolen from the central bank. The Hawks, a South African police unit, said Lesotho officials intercepted vouchers meant for service providers and diverted the payments to co-conspirators in South Africa. They also said some officials were already before court in Lesotho. The charges are allegations, and no outcome is reported.
n:Parliamentary inquiry commission on No: This is a Portuguese parliamentary commission, based in Lisbon, that investigated the losses of Novo Banco. It is tied to the Bank of Portugal, the central bank, as its investigator. On 20 July 2021 the commission's rapporteur, Fernando Anastácio, presented a proposed final report saying supervision failed across the board and that there was a permanent and systematic failure. This was a draft. The PSD party said its deputies would vote against it and propose amendments.
n:Fernando Anastácio: Fernando Anastácio is a Portuguese politician who was rapporteur of the parliamentary inquiry into Novo Banco's losses. He is tied to the Bank of Portugal, the central bank, as an investigator. On 20 July 2021 he presented a proposed final report saying supervision failed across the board and that there was a permanent and systematic failure. This was a draft. The PSD party said its deputies would vote against it and propose amendments.
n:Cristina Kirchner: Cristina Kirchner was President of Argentina. She is tied to the Central Bank of the Argentine Republic through the removal of its governor, Martin Redrado. On 6 January the government called on him to resign, saying he refused to back its decree calling for 6.6 billion dollars of reserves. He refused to go. On 7 January Kirchner issued a second decree firing him and accusing him of misconduct. On 8 January the courts suspended both decrees.
n:Argentine courts: The Argentine courts are named in an event involving the Central Bank of the Argentine Republic. On 6 January the government called on the bank's governor, Martin Redrado, to resign, saying he refused to back its decree calling for 6.6 billion dollars of reserves. He refused to go. On 7 January President Kirchner issued a second decree firing him and accusing him of misconduct. On 8 January the courts suspended both decrees.
n:Goodluck Jonathan: Goodluck Jonathan was President of Nigeria. He is tied to the Central Bank of Nigeria through the suspension of its governor, Sanusi Lamido Sanusi. The president's aide cited "various acts of financial recklessness". Sanusi had reported the year before that 50 billion dollars of oil sold by the state oil company NNPC had not been paid to the government. NNPC repeatedly denied his allegations. Sanusi could not be reached for comment on the suspension.
n:Government of India: The Government of India, based in New Delhi, is tied to the Reserve Bank of India, the central bank. Governor Urjit Patel resigned, saying only that it was for personal reasons. Media reports said he was annoyed by repeated government efforts to influence central bank policy, after a public spat over alleged interference. Finance Minister Arun Jaitley responded by acknowledging Patel's time at the bank with appreciation.
n:Council of Representatives of Iraq: The Council of Representatives is Iraq's parliament, based in Baghdad. It is tied to the Central Bank of Iraq. Governor Sinan Al Shabibi was removed and a successor named during a parliamentary probe into possible manipulation of the dinar against the dollar. A committee member said arrest warrants had been issued for 30 people, including Al Shabibi and his deputy, Mudher Saleh. The integrity committee chairman said the probe was "not about money, but about procedures". A finance committee member called it "a political decision and not professional". The article reports no statement from Al Shabibi.
n:Thaksin Shinawatra: Thaksin Shinawatra was Prime Minister of Thailand. He is tied to the Bank of Thailand, the central bank, through the firing of its governor, Chatu Mongol Sonakul. The government fired the governor, and Thaksin said he was not satisfied with the bank's policy of keeping interest rates low. The article carries no response from the governor.
n:President of Cyprus: The President of Cyprus, based in Nicosia, is tied to the Central Bank of Cyprus. Governor Panicos Demetriades resigned, to leave on 10 April, with no reason given. The president had earlier said he would begin proceedings to have him removed for not doing his job properly. At the resignation a government statement thanked him for helping prevent the country's bankruptcy. The article carries no statement from Demetriades on the dispute.
n:Attorney General of Indonesia: The Attorney General of Indonesia leads the country's prosecutors, based in Jakarta. It is tied to Bank Indonesia, the central bank, through the case of Governor Syahril. He was released after six months of detention when prosecutors' detention orders expired. He faced corruption charges and a possible life sentence over his alleged involvement in the 546 billion rupiah Bank Bali scandal, while the administration was pushing to remove him. A presidential spokesman said "This release merely follows legal procedures". A Jakarta court sentenced him to three years in 2002. In 2004 Kyodo, quoting a senior Supreme Court judge, reported that the top court rejected prosecutors' appeal and acquitted him on all charges.
n:Government of Indonesia: The Government of Indonesia, based in Jakarta, is tied to Bank Indonesia, the central bank, through the case of Governor Syahril. He was released after six months of detention when prosecutors' detention orders expired. He faced corruption charges and a possible life sentence over his alleged involvement in the 546 billion rupiah Bank Bali scandal, while the administration was pushing to remove him and install its own candidates. A presidential spokesman said "This release merely follows legal procedures". A Jakarta court sentenced him to three years in 2002. In 2004 Kyodo, quoting a senior Supreme Court judge, reported that the top court rejected prosecutors' appeal and acquitted him on all charges.
n:Joyce Banda: Joyce Banda was President of Malawi. She is tied to the Reserve Bank of Malawi, the central bank. According to two unnamed sources, she removed its governor, Perks Ligoya, with Charles Chuka reportedly chosen to succeed him. No official reason was stated. The reporter described it as her latest move to clean house and woo donors back. No one at the central bank was available for comment.
n:President of Sierra Leone: The President of Sierra Leone, based in Freetown, is tied to the Bank of Sierra Leone, the central bank. The recently elected president dismissed the governor, and Kelfala Kallon was appointed on 15 August as the bank's third governor in 17 months. The dismissed governor and the reason are not recorded.
n:Julius Maada Bio: Julius Maada Bio is President of Sierra Leone. He is tied to the Bank of Sierra Leone, the central bank. He sent governor Kelfala Kallon on "indefinite leave" and named deputy Ibrahim Stevens interim head. The advisory firm that wrote the article reports no official reason and no response from Kallon. It says the president tried to bypass the 2019 Bank of Sierra Leone Act, under which sacking the governor needs a two-thirds majority in parliament.
n:Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine: The Verkhovna Rada is Ukraine's parliament, based in Kyiv. It is tied to the National Bank of Ukraine, the central bank. Parliament voted no confidence in the bank's head, Volodymyr Stelmakh, with 227 of 450 seats in favour. It cited a fall of nearly half in the hryvna's value since November, a shrinking economy and rising deficits. President Yushchenko's office called the decision "illegal" and repeated its support for Stelmakh.
n:Moncef Marzouki: Moncef Marzouki was President of Tunisia. He is tied to the Central Bank of Tunisia through the firing of its governor, Mustapha Kamel Nabli. Marzouki alleged Nabli had refused to bring monetary policy in line with the country's economic needs. The elected assembly approved the move in July 2012. The article carries no statement from Nabli.
n:National Constituent Assembly of Tunis: The National Constituent Assembly is Tunisia's elected assembly, based in Tunis. It is tied to the Central Bank of Tunisia. President Moncef Marzouki fired central bank governor Mustapha Kamel Nabli, alleging he had refused to bring monetary policy in line with the country's economic needs. The assembly approved the move in July 2012. The article carries no statement from Nabli.
n:Ministry of Finance of Belize: The Ministry of Finance of Belize, based in Belmopan, is tied to the Central Bank of Belize. Governor Gustavo Manuel Vasquez lost his post. Prime Minister John Briceño said the board recommended he resign because of "a lot of policy differences". Vasquez wrote that his appointment was terminated on the instructions of the Ministry of Finance and that he faced opposition from it. He wrote that he had tried to restore the bank's integrity and operational autonomy.
n:John Briceño: John Briceño is Prime Minister of Belize. He is tied to the Central Bank of Belize through the loss of its governor's post. Gustavo Manuel Vasquez lost the job. Briceño said the board recommended he resign because of "a lot of policy differences". Vasquez wrote that his appointment was terminated on the instructions of the Ministry of Finance, that he faced opposition from it, and that he had tried to restore the bank's integrity and operational autonomy.
n:Movement for Democratic Change: The Movement for Democratic Change (MDC) is a political party in Zimbabwe. It is tied to the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe, the central bank. As a partner in the power-sharing government, it demanded that governor Gideon Gono be replaced, saying Western donors would not fund reconstruction until he was. President Mugabe said Gono would stay: "Prove the wrong he has done." Gono reportedly sought protection from "personal attacks" by Finance Minister Tendai Biti. Gono was not removed in this account.
n:Tendai Biti: Tendai Biti was Finance Minister of Zimbabwe. He is tied to the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe, the central bank. His party, the Movement for Democratic Change, was a partner in the power-sharing government and demanded that governor Gideon Gono be replaced, saying Western donors would not fund reconstruction until he was. President Mugabe said Gono would stay: "Prove the wrong he has done." Gono reportedly sought protection from "personal attacks" by Biti. Gono was not removed in this account.
n:Maithripala Sirisena: Maithripala Sirisena was President of Sri Lanka. He is tied to the Central Bank of Sri Lanka through its governor, Arjuna Mahendran. In June 2015 Sirisena said Mahendran should resign. Mahendran's term ended on 30 June, and he told the Monetary Board he would not seek reappointment until the parliamentary committee COPE finished its Treasury bond probe. Sirisena tweeted he would appoint a new governor within hours. Prime Minister Ranil Wickremesinghe said Mahendran could not be removed because the charges "had never been proved". The Auditor General found a loss of 1.6 billion rupees. In a later speech Sirisena said he personally removed Mahendran, citing the national interest.
n:Fiscalía General del Estado de Bolivia: The Fiscalía General del Estado is Bolivia's state prosecutor's office. It is tied to the Central Bank of Bolivia. Guillermo Aponte became interim president of the bank, replacing Pablo Ramos, who was under investigation for alleged favouring of illicit enrichment. The questions covered armoured trucks said to have taken foreign currency out of the bank at unusual hours and about 75 million dollars in loans to state firms. Ramos is under investigation, which is not a finding of guilt. The article has no statement from him.
n:Jeanine Áñez: Jeanine Áñez was transitional president of Bolivia. She is tied to the Central Bank of Bolivia. Guillermo Aponte became interim president of the bank, replacing Pablo Ramos, who was under investigation for alleged favouring of illicit enrichment. The questions covered armoured trucks said to have taken foreign currency out of the bank at unusual hours and about 75 million dollars in loans to state firms. Áñez said the bank "recupera la autonomía de decisión". Ramos is under investigation, which is not a finding of guilt. The article has no statement from him.
n:Government of São Tomé and Príncipe: The Government of São Tomé and Príncipe is tied to the Central Bank of São Tomé and Príncipe. It dismissed governor Maria do Carmo Silveira, a former prime minister, and her team. It cited irregularities in the construction of the new central bank building, valued at 8 million US dollars. The article does not mention corruption or fraud.
n:BNP Paribas: BNP Paribas is a bank based in Paris, France, tied to two central banks. It is listed as having paid Janet Yellen, Fed chair until early 2018, for speeches or advice after she left the Federal Reserve System, the central bank of the United States. François Villeroy de Galhau was Chief Operating Officer of the BNP Paribas group before becoming Governor of the Banque de France, the French central bank, on 1 November 2015.
n:ING: ING is a bank based in Amsterdam, Netherlands. It is listed as having paid Janet Yellen, Fed chair until early 2018, for speeches or advice after she left the Federal Reserve System, the central bank of the United States, based on her disclosed speaking income as of January 2021.
n:Standard Chartered: Standard Chartered is a bank based in London, United Kingdom, tied to one central bank and one other body. It is listed as having paid Janet Yellen, Fed chair until early 2018, for speeches or advice after she left the Federal Reserve System, the central bank of the United States. Maria Ramos represents it in the Group of Thirty, a forum where central bankers also sit; the source lists her as Chair and notes she has been Senior Independent Director since 2022.
n:City National Bank: City National Bank is a bank based in Los Angeles, United States. It is listed as having paid Janet Yellen, Fed chair until early 2018, for speeches or advice after she left the Federal Reserve System, the central bank of the United States, based on her disclosed speaking income as of January 2021.
n:Bank of America: Bank of America is a bank based in Charlotte, United States, tied to two central banks. CNN named it among the firms listed in Janet Yellen's financial disclosures, which showed more than $7 million from speeches in recent years; she chaired the Federal Reserve until early 2018. A profile of Agus Martowardojo, elected governor of Bank Indonesia in 2013, lists a post at Bank of America in 1984. No ethics finding is recorded.
n:Wells Fargo: Wells Fargo is a bank based in San Francisco, United States. It is tied to the Federal Reserve System, the central bank of the United States, through one person's career. Elizabeth Duke went from Fed governor to Wells Fargo director, then chair of its board. William F. Ford was its chief economist, a vice president in 1975 and senior vice president in 1977, before becoming president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta on 1 August 1980.
n:American National Bank: American National Bank is a bank based in Omaha, United States. It is tied to the Federal Reserve System, the central bank of the United States, through one person's career. Jeffrey R. Schmid, now President of the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City, was president of American National Bank and of Mutual of Omaha's banking entry before that post.
n:Mutual of Omaha: Mutual of Omaha is a company based in Omaha, United States. It is tied to the Federal Reserve System, the central bank of the United States, through one person's career. Jeffrey R. Schmid, now President of the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City, was president of American National Bank and of Mutual of Omaha's banking entry before that post.
n:BlueMountain Capital Management: BlueMountain Capital Management is a company based in New York, United States. It is listed as having paid a former official of the Federal Reserve System, the central bank of the United States: Jeremy C. Stein, a Fed governor from May 2012 to May 2014, became a consultant to the firm.
n:Paulson & Co: Paulson & Co is a company based in New York, United States. It is listed as having paid a former official of the Federal Reserve System, the central bank of the United States: Alan Greenspan, a former Fed chairman, joined the firm's advisory board.
n:Swiss Re: Swiss Re is a company based in Zurich, Switzerland, tied to two central banks through the careers of two people. Roger W. Ferguson Jr., Fed vice chairman from October 1999 to April 2006, was a McKinsey partner until 1987, later Fed vice chairman, then on the Swiss Re executive board. Sir Paul Tucker went from Deputy Governor of the Bank of England, the United Kingdom's central bank (2009 to 2013), to the Swiss Re board of directors.
n:TIAA: TIAA is a company based in New York, United States. It is tied to the Federal Reserve System, the central bank of the United States, through one person's career. Roger W. Ferguson Jr., Fed vice chairman from October 1999 to April 2006, was a McKinsey partner until 1987, later Fed vice chairman, then moved to the Swiss Re executive board and to TIAA.
n:Rabobank: Rabobank is a bank based in Utrecht, Netherlands. It is tied to De Nederlandsche Bank, the Dutch central bank, through one person's career. Wim Duisenberg worked on the staff of the International Monetary Fund, then on the Rabobank board, then became chairman of De Nederlandsche Bank from 1982.
n:Autonomous Research: Autonomous Research is a company based in London. Sir Paul Tucker, Deputy Governor of the Bank of England from 2009 to 2013, is listed on its Advisory Committee in his Swiss Re CV. No ethics finding is recorded.
n:Infrastructure Development Finance Com: The Infrastructure Development Finance Company is based in Chennai, India. It is tied to the Reserve Bank of India, the country's central bank, through one person's career. Urjit Patel worked at the International Monetary Fund, IDFC, Reliance Industries and Boston Consulting Group before becoming Deputy Governor of the central bank in January 2013.
n:Macquarie Group: Macquarie Group is a company based in Sydney, Australia. It is tied to the Reserve Bank of Australia, the country's central bank, through one person's career. Glenn Stevens, RBA governor from 2006 to 2016, became an independent director of Macquarie Group.
n:Nubank: Nubank is a company based in São Paulo, Brazil. Roberto Campos Neto, president of the Central Bank of Brazil (the country's central bank) from 2019 to the end of 2024, worked at Santander and other private finance firms before the post, then became vice chairman of Nubank.
n:Santander: Santander is a bank based in Santander, Spain. Roberto Campos Neto, president of the Central Bank of Brazil (the country's central bank) from 2019 to the end of 2024, worked at Santander and other private finance firms before the post, then became vice chairman of Nubank.
n:Claritas Investments: Claritas Investments is an investment firm based in Sao Paulo, Brazil. Roberto Campos Neto, president of the Central Bank of Brazil from 2019 to the end of 2024, held a leadership role there before taking office, according to a Nubank announcement of May 2025. He became Nubank's vice chairman after a six-month cooling-off period set by Brazilian law. No ethics finding is recorded.
n:Bozano Simonsen: Bozano Simonsen is a bank based in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Roberto Campos Neto, president of the Central Bank of Brazil from 2019 to the end of 2024, held a leadership role there before taking office, according to a Nubank announcement of May 2025. He became Nubank's vice chairman after a six-month cooling-off period set by Brazilian law. No ethics finding is recorded.
n:Itaú Unibanco: Itaú Unibanco is a bank based in São Paulo, Brazil. It is tied to the Central Bank of Brazil, the country's central bank, through one person's career. Ilan Goldfajn, Governor from May 2016 to February 2019, also held roles at Itaú Unibanco, Credit Suisse Brazil and the International Monetary Fund; the source gives no order for these moves relative to his time at the central bank.
n:BankBoston: BankBoston is a bank based in Boston, United States. Henrique de Campos Meirelles, president of the Central Bank of Brazil (the country's central bank) from 2003 to 2010, also held roles at BankBoston, FleetBoston and Lazard Americas; the source gives no order for these moves relative to his time at the central bank.
n:FleetBoston: FleetBoston is a bank based in Boston, United States. Henrique de Campos Meirelles, president of the Central Bank of Brazil (the country's central bank) from 2003 to 2010, also held roles at BankBoston, FleetBoston and Lazard Americas; the source gives no order for these moves relative to his time at the central bank.
n:Grupo Financiero Banorte: Grupo Financiero Banorte is a bank based in Monterrey, Mexico. It is tied to the Bank of Mexico, the country's central bank, through one person's career. Guillermo Ortiz went from governor of the Bank of Mexico to chairman of BTG Pactual Mexico, and was also a former chairman of Grupo Financiero Banorte.
n:Santiago Peña: Santiago Peña is the president of Paraguay. He is tied to the Central Bank of Paraguay, the country's central bank, through the resignation of its head, Carlos Carvallo, who stepped down at Peña's request. Peña said he asked "in light of facts that emerged throughout the day". Those included a prosecutor's request for a criminal investigation around the digital lender ueno and orders to arrest eight people linked to it. Carvallo said stepping aside would help quell the controversy around the bank. He had headed ueno until August 2023, and Peña was a business partner of the group that owned it until March 2025.
n:Nicanor Duarte Frutos: Nicanor Duarte Frutos was president of Paraguay. He dismissed Mónica Pérez, president of the Central Bank of Paraguay, a former official of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) who had been in the post since June 2005. An unnamed official source said the reason was her constant disagreements with the rest of the government's economic team. No response from Pérez is given.
n:Nursultan Nazarbayev: Nursultan Nazarbayev was president of Kazakhstan. He replaced the chairman of the National Bank of Kazakhstan, Kayrat Kelimbetov, with a presidential adviser, Daniyar Akishev. Nazarbayev told parliament that confidence in the bank and in the tenge, the national currency, had fallen and that a shortage of tenge liquidity was being felt. No statement from Kelimbetov is given.
n:Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi: Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi was president of Yemen. Announcing from Saudi Arabia, he sacked the head of the Central Bank of Yemen, Mohammed bin Hammam, named Mansar al-Kaiti in his place and ordered the bank moved to Aden. No official reason was quoted, and neither bin Hammam nor the Houthis responded. The move was described as one that would raise pressure on the Houthi rebels, who hold the capital.
n:Parliament of Moldova: The Parliament of Moldova is the country's legislature, based in Chișinău. On the evening of 21 December it dismissed Octavian Armașu, governor of the National Bank of Moldova since November 2018, with 81 members voting in favour. This followed hearings on recovering money stolen from the banking system. The decision cited "insufficient and defective work" by the bank in examining the bank fraud case. No response from Armașu is given.
n:Kittiratt Na-Ranong: Kittiratt Na-Ranong was Thailand's finance minister. He said the governor of the Bank of Thailand, Prasarn Trairatvorakul, should be replaced because he had not cut the repurchase rate, the bank's main interest rate, to slow the baht's rise. Kittiratt called the 2.75% rate too high. Prasarn was unavailable for comment. Korn Chatikavanij said Kittiratt should not have spoken out, because it could erode investor confidence.
n:Parliament of Georgia: The Parliament of Georgia voted 80 to 19 to move banking supervision away from the National Bank of Georgia and into a new Financial Supervisory Agency. The draft came from two MPs of the Georgian Dream party. One of them, Tamaz Mechiauri, reportedly argued that the makeup of the National Bank's board was against the current leadership's interests and that the change would discourage currency speculation. Bidzina Ivanishvili blamed the bank and its chairman, Giorgi Kadagidze, for the fall of the lari, the national currency. No statement from Kadagidze is given.
n:Tamaz Mechiauri: Tamaz Mechiauri is a Georgian Dream member of the Parliament of Georgia and co-author of a bill that moved banking supervision from the National Bank of Georgia to a new Financial Supervisory Agency. Parliament passed it 80 to 19. He reportedly argued that the National Bank board's makeup was against the current leadership's interests and that the change would discourage currency speculation. Bidzina Ivanishvili blamed the bank and its chairman, Giorgi Kadagidze, for the fall of the lari. No statement from Kadagidze is given.
n:Nodar Ebanoidze: Nodar Ebanoidze, in Georgia, is tied to the National Bank of Georgia through a parliamentary vote of 80 to 19 that moved banking supervision from the bank to a new Financial Supervisory Agency. The bill was drafted by two Georgian Dream MPs. One of them, Tamaz Mechiauri, reportedly said the bank board's makeup was against the current leadership's interests. Bidzina Ivanishvili blamed the bank and its chairman, Giorgi Kadagidze, for the fall of the lari. No statement from Kadagidze is given.
n:Bidzina Ivanishvili: Bidzina Ivanishvili is tied to the National Bank of Georgia through a dispute over the lari, the national currency. He blamed the bank and its chairman, Giorgi Kadagidze, for the lari's fall. Parliament then voted 80 to 19 to move banking supervision from the bank to a new Financial Supervisory Agency, on a draft from two Georgian Dream MPs. One of them, Tamaz Mechiauri, reportedly argued that the board's makeup was against the current leadership's interests. No statement from Kadagidze is given.
n:Ilham Aliyev: Ilham Aliyev is president of Azerbaijan. Parliament approved his proposal to replace Elman Rustamov, governor of the Central Bank of the Republic of Azerbaijan since 1995, with Taleh Kazimov, head of Pasha Bank. Rustamov was then made an adviser to the prime minister. No official reason and no statement from Rustamov is given.
n:Parliament of Azerbaijan: The Parliament of Azerbaijan sits in Baku. It approved President Ilham Aliyev's proposal to replace Elman Rustamov, governor of the Central Bank of the Republic of Azerbaijan since 1995, with Taleh Kazimov, head of Pasha Bank. Rustamov was then made an adviser to the prime minister. No official reason and no statement from Rustamov is given.
n:Daniel Chapo: Daniel Chapo is president of Mozambique. He revoked the appointment of Waldemar Fernando de Sousa as governor of the Bank of Mozambique "due to subsequent circumstances", which the statement did not specify, and named Felisberto Dinis Navalha instead. The article says Chapo may have backed down after public criticism, because the Attorney General's Office accuses De Sousa of involvement in the hidden debts scandal. De Sousa was not tried in the main case. No response from him is given.
n:Attorney General's Office of Mozambiqu: The Attorney General's Office of Mozambique is a state prosecuting body. It accuses Waldemar Fernando de Sousa of involvement in the hidden debts scandal, though he was not tried in the main case. President Daniel Chapo revoked De Sousa's appointment as governor of the Bank of Mozambique "due to subsequent circumstances", which the statement did not specify, and named Felisberto Dinis Navalha instead. The article says Chapo may have backed down after public criticism. No response from De Sousa is given.
n:Filipe Nyusi: Filipe Nyusi was president of Mozambique. He fired António Pinto de Abreu, deputy governor of the Bank of Mozambique, who had been in the post since December 2010. The president's office gave no reason.
n:Isaac Adongo: Isaac Adongo is a member of Ghana's Parliament who spoke for the Minority, the opposition members. He called Ernest Addison, governor of the Bank of Ghana, "incompetent" over the fall of the cedi and over inflation, and said Addison should resign or be sacked. He said Addison had borrowed "in excess of 7billion dollars" on the bank's balance sheet to support the cedi, and claimed the government had borrowed illegally through the bank. No answer from the governor or the government is given.
n:Minority in Parliament of Ghana: The Minority in Parliament of Ghana is the group of opposition members. Speaking for it, Isaac Adongo called Ernest Addison, governor of the Bank of Ghana, "incompetent" over the fall of the cedi and over inflation, and said he should resign or be sacked. Adongo said Addison had borrowed "in excess of 7billion dollars" on the bank's balance sheet to support the cedi, and claimed the government had borrowed illegally through the bank. No answer from the governor or the government is given.
n:Kwasi Ameyaw-Cheremeh: Kwasi Ameyaw-Cheremeh is a member of Ghana's Parliament. He said the government forced Henry Kofi Wampah out as governor of the Bank of Ghana because of embarrassments including the micro-finance crisis in Brong Ahafo. This is his claim and is not confirmed. Wampah said he had agreed with President Mahama to leave at the end of March, ahead of his August term end, so a successor could settle in before the elections. No government response is given.
n:Rodrigo Duterte: Rodrigo Duterte was president of the Philippines. In a speech announcing the 2017 budget, he told Amando Tetangco, governor of Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, the central bank, "I will give you a whack". He also threatened criminal charges against the Anti-Money Laundering Council, which Tetangco chairs, accusing it of not tracking drug money, without giving details of the alleged corruption. Tetangco did not immediately respond. Deputy Governor Diwa Guinigundo said the bank was independent.
n:Ranil Wickremesinghe: Ranil Wickremesinghe was prime minister of Sri Lanka. The term of Arjuna Mahendran, governor of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka, ended on 30 June. Mahendran told the Monetary Board he would not seek reappointment until the parliamentary committee COPE finished its probe of a Treasury bond sale. President Maithripala Sirisena, who said in June 2015 that Mahendran should resign, tweeted that he would appoint a new governor within hours. Wickremesinghe said Mahendran could not be removed because the charges "had never been proved". The Auditor General found a loss of 1.6 billion rupees. No new governor was announced that day.
n:Committee on Public Enterprises (COPE): The Committee on Public Enterprises (COPE) is a committee of Sri Lanka's parliament. It was investigating a Treasury bond sale at the Central Bank of Sri Lanka. The bank's governor, Arjuna Mahendran, whose term ended on 30 June, told the Monetary Board he would not seek reappointment until COPE finished. President Maithripala Sirisena, who said in June 2015 that Mahendran should resign, tweeted that he would name a new governor within hours. Prime Minister Ranil Wickremesinghe said Mahendran could not be removed because the charges "had never been proved". The Auditor General found a loss of 1.6 billion rupees. No new governor was announced that day.
n:Auditor General of Sri Lanka: The Auditor General of Sri Lanka audits the accounts of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka, including those for the year ended 31 December 2024, and the Auditor General's Department published that report. In the Treasury bond matter, the Auditor General found a loss of 1.6 billion rupees. The bank's governor, Arjuna Mahendran, whose term ended on 30 June, said he would not seek reappointment until the parliamentary committee COPE finished its probe. Prime Minister Ranil Wickremesinghe said Mahendran could not be removed because the charges "had never been proved". No new governor was announced that day.
n:Fiscalía de La Paz: The Fiscalía de La Paz is the prosecutors' office in La Paz, Bolivia. It ordered the arrest of Edwin Rojas, a former president of the Central Bank of Bolivia, and three former executives. They are investigated for breach of duties and uneconomic conduct over a 2024 regulation that the prosecutor says allowed irregular sovereign bond transactions, with alleged damage of 124 million US dollars. These are allegations and are unproven. Rojas invoked his right to silence. No formal charge is reported.
n:Ishaq Dar: Ishaq Dar was Pakistan's finance minister. Yaseen Anwar, governor of the State Bank of Pakistan, resigned. The Finance Ministry spokesman said he cited personal reasons. Unnamed senior officials said that was a cover for differences with Dar over inflation and reserves, and that Anwar was unhappy with a recent deputy governor appointment. The article reports no government pressure.
n:Parliament of Kyrgyzstan: The Parliament of Kyrgyzstan sits in Bishkek. It approved the resignation letter of Kubanychbek Bokontaev, head of the National Bank of the Kyrgyz Republic since 2021, which relieved him ahead of schedule. The article gives no reason from either side.
n:Government of Argentina: The Government of Argentina, based in Buenos Aires, was to replace Alfonso Prat-Gay, president of the Central Bank of the Argentine Republic, with Martin Redrado. Prat-Gay's term ended that week, and the appointment needed Senate approval. This was under President Néstor Kirchner. The article says the trigger was unclear, and local media suggested disagreements over the debt restructuring. Neither side is quoted.
n:Zoran Djindjic: Zoran Djindjic was prime minister of Serbia. A bill expected to pass on 15 July would place the National Bank of Serbia under government control and allow the dismissal of its governor, Mladjan Dinkic. The government side complained that Djindjic wanted a devaluation, a deliberate cut in the currency's value, that Dinkic resisted, and members of DOS said a party official cannot be governor. Dinkic said the law would make the bank dependent on government and parliament. Authorities said his claims had no foundation.
n:DOS: DOS is a political group in Serbia. A bill expected to pass on 15 July would place the National Bank of Serbia under government control and allow the dismissal of its governor, Mladjan Dinkic. DOS members said a party official cannot be governor, and Prime Minister Zoran Djindjic wanted a devaluation, a deliberate cut in the currency's value, that Dinkic resisted. Dinkic said the law would make the bank dependent on government and parliament. Authorities said his claims had no foundation.
n:Abul Maal Abdul Muhith: Abul Maal Abdul Muhith was Bangladesh's finance minister. Atiur Rahman, governor of Bangladesh Bank, resigned after a hack that cost 81 million dollars, saying he was "ready to resign from my post for the sake of the country". Rahman had been criticised for not telling the finance minister about the loss, and Muhith called the bank's handling very incompetent.
n:Mahathir: Mahathir led Malaysia's government during the Asian Financial Crisis. Bank Negara Malaysia's governor, Ahmad Mohd Don, and his deputy, Fong Weng Phak, resigned "as a matter of principle". The article says Ahmad Don favoured tight monetary policy, backed by Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim, while Mahathir and Daim Zainuddin wanted an expansionary approach, meaning looser money. It says Anwar was sacked over the dispute.
n:Daim Zainuddin: Daim Zainuddin is named in the account of the resignations at Bank Negara Malaysia during the Asian Financial Crisis. Governor Ahmad Mohd Don and his deputy, Fong Weng Phak, resigned "as a matter of principle". The article says Ahmad Don favoured tight monetary policy, backed by Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim, while Mahathir and Daim wanted an expansionary approach, meaning looser money. It says Anwar was sacked over the dispute.
n:Boris Yeltsin: Boris Yeltsin was president of Russia. He fired Viktor Gerashchenko, chairman of the Bank of Russia, for his role in the Black Tuesday ruble crash and appointed Tatyana Paramonova in his place. The State Duma, the lower house of parliament, then rejected her in a secret ballot, 107 to 127. Opponents said the constitution barred hiring or firing the bank's chief without Duma approval.
n:State Duma: The State Duma is the lower house of Russia's parliament, in Moscow. President Boris Yeltsin fired Viktor Gerashchenko, chairman of the Bank of Russia, for his role in the Black Tuesday ruble crash and appointed Tatyana Paramonova. The Duma rejected her in a secret ballot, 107 to 127. Opponents said the constitution barred hiring or firing the bank's chief without Duma approval.
n:Centralne Biuro Antykorupcyjne: The Centralne Biuro Antykorupcyjne is Poland's Central Anti-Corruption Bureau, based in Warsaw. In February 2009 it said its officers detained eight people in a case against a division head in the IT and telecommunications department of the National Bank of Poland. He was accused of taking bribes worth at least 350,000 zloty to rig tenders between 2001 and 2008. Prosecutors charged the businessmen who ran an IT systems firm with giving him bribes. The accusations are unproven, and no outcome is given.
n:Bahrain High Criminal Court: The Bahrain High Criminal Court is a court in Bahrain. Asharq Al-Awsat reported in November 2020 that it fined the Central Bank of Iran and other Iran-owned banks, including Future Bank, 1 million Bahraini dinars each, and jailed three Future Bank officials for five years. Prosecutors said the Central Bank of Iran planned to launder billions of dollars through Future Bank. They said Future Bank handled suspicious SWIFT transfers, a bank-to-bank messaging system, that favored Iranian entities, mainly the central bank, without reporting them.
n:Bahrain Public Prosecution: The Bahrain Public Prosecution is the prosecuting body in Bahrain. It said the Central Bank of Iran planned to launder billions of dollars through Future Bank, which handled suspicious SWIFT transfers, a bank-to-bank messaging system, that favored Iranian entities, mainly the central bank, without reporting them. n:Future Bank: Future Bank is one of the Iran-owned banks fined in Bahrain. n:Laurent Gbagbo: Laurent Gbagbo was president of Côte d'Ivoire. On 18 January 2018 a court in Côte d'Ivoire, with judge Sombé Méïté giving the verdict, sentenced Gbagbo, Aké N'Gbo, Katinan and Dallo to 20 years in prison and a fine of 329 billion CFA francs. The offences included group theft by break-in of vaults and cash of the Central Bank of West African States (BCEAO) during the post-election crisis from December 2010 to April 2011. Seven bailiffs got 36 months and a fine of 700,000 CFA francs. Katinan was absent throughout the trial. Gbagbo always denied the charges, and President Ouattara pardoned him on 6 August 2022.
n:Union Économique et Monétaire Ouest-Af: The Union Économique et Monétaire Ouest-Africaine (UEMOA) is the West African economic and monetary union, based in Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso. A summit of its heads of state accepted the resignation of Dacoury-Tabley, governor of the Central Bank of West African States (BCEAO), in January 2011. He was criticized for ignoring a 23 December decision by UEMOA finance ministers that gave Alassane Ouattara power over the institution. The article says the BCEAO paid 60 to 100 billion CFA francs to the Gbagbo regime after that date. Senegal's President Abdoulaye Wade asked for an audit and alleged the former governor moved 500 billion CFA francs to Gbagbo after being dismissed. Another figure cited is 300 billion. That report gives no audit result.
n:Laurent Gbagbo government: The Laurent Gbagbo government ruled from Abidjan, Côte d'Ivoire. One article says the Central Bank of West African States (BCEAO) paid 60 to 100 billion CFA francs to the Gbagbo regime after a 23 December decision by finance ministers of the West African monetary union gave Alassane Ouattara power over the institution. The bank's governor, Dacoury-Tabley, resigned in January 2011 and was criticized for ignoring that decision. Senegal's President Abdoulaye Wade asked for an audit and alleged the former governor moved 500 billion CFA francs to Gbagbo after being dismissed. Another figure cited is 300 billion. That report gives no audit result.
n:Directorate of Public Prosecutions (Bo: The Directorate of Public Prosecutions of Botswana is the state prosecuting body. A woman arrested on 17 October 2019 was implicated, with others including former president Ian Khama and former intelligence head Isaac Kgosi, in allegedly stealing 100 billion pula from the Bank of Botswana. High Court Judge Zein Kebonang discharged and acquitted her of unexplained property and a false passport declaration. The state withdrew a terrorism financing charge. He found the accusations fabricated and referred the investigator to police for perjury prosecution.
n:Directorate on Corruption and Economic: The Directorate on Corruption and Economic Crime is Botswana's anti-corruption agency. n:High Court of Botswana: The High Court of Botswana heard the case of a woman arrested on 17 October 2019, who was implicated with others, including former president Ian Khama and former intelligence head Isaac Kgosi, in allegedly stealing 100 billion pula from the Bank of Botswana. Judge Zein Kebonang discharged and acquitted her of unexplained property and a false passport declaration. The state withdrew a terrorism financing charge. n:Anti-Corruption Commission (Sierra Leo: The Anti-Corruption Commission is Sierra Leone's anti-corruption agency, based in Freetown. On 22 November 2021 Governor Kallon of the Bank of Sierra Leone told Parliament he had "bribed" people hoarding the leone to bring it back into the banking system. The Commission investigated. In May 2022 it said he was referring to cash swap operations in which the bank sold about 68.6 million US dollars in foreign currency in 2021, and that the word was used in error. It closed the investigation after advising him to choose his words more carefully.
n:KfW: KfW, a bank based in Frankfurt, Germany, shares people with the Deutsche Bundesbank, Germany's central bank. Joachim Nagel, a Bundesbank Executive Board member from 2010 to 2016 and its President since January 2022, moved from the Bundesbank Executive Board to the KfW Executive Board.
n:Bank for International Settlements: The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) is based in Basel, Switzerland, and is tied to 63 central banks. Those 63 own it; its capital is held by central banks only, and private shares were bought back in 2001. Examples are the Bank of Algeria, the Central Bank of the Argentine Republic and the Reserve Bank of Australia. It also appears in the revolving-door record of the Deutsche Bundesbank: Joachim Nagel, Bundesbank Executive Board member 2010-2016 and President since January 2022, moved to the KfW Executive Board and later to the BIS.
n:Merrill Lynch: Merrill Lynch, a bank in New York, employed an official of the Bank of Israel, Israel's central bank. Jacob Frenkel, Governor of the Bank of Israel 1991-2000, went from International Monetary Fund Economic Counselor to Bank of Israel Governor, then became chairman of Merrill Lynch International. Riad Salameh worked at the firm from 1973 to 1993, managing the personal portfolio of Rafic Hariri, who as prime minister appointed him governor of the Banque du Liban in 1993.
n:AIG: AIG, a company in New York, employed an official of the Bank of Israel, Israel's central bank. The source gives a career path, not an accusation.
n:JPMorgan Chase: JPMorgan Chase, a bank in New York, employed an official of the Bank of Israel, Israel's central bank. n:Absa Group: Absa Group, a bank in Johannesburg, South Africa, shares people with the South African Reserve Bank. The source records a career move, not an accusation.
n:Permodalan Nasional Berhad: Permodalan Nasional Berhad, a company in Kuala Lumpur, employed an official of Bank Negara Malaysia, the central bank of Malaysia. Zeti Akhtar Aziz, who headed the central bank for 16 years and retired in 2016, went from Bank Negara governor to group chairman of Permodalan Nasional Berhad. The source records a career move, not an accusation.
n:Bank Mandiri: Bank Mandiri, a bank in Jakarta, shares people with Bank Indonesia, the central bank. Destry Damayanti, Senior Deputy Governor 2019-2026 and Governor from 2 September 2026, came from Chief Economist at Mandiri Sekuritas and Bank Mandiri.

n:Crane AB: Crane AB is a banknote printer based in Tumba, Sweden, tied to three central banks. It printed Swedish banknotes at Tumba, a plant it bought from Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, in 2002. On 19 June 2018 the Riksbank gave notice to end the contract because Crane was moving printing to Malta. In 2017 Brazil's central bank contracted it for 100 million notes of 2 reais, at a cost of 20.2 million reais. In Kenya, Crane challenged the central bank's award of a new currency printing tender to De La Rue as irregular and not transparent. The Central Bank of Kenya rejected those claims.
n:Oberthur Fiduciaire: Oberthur Fiduciaire is a banknote printer based in Paris, France, tied to two central banks. Denmark's central bank, Danmarks Nationalbank, selected it as its new banknote supplier under a four-year framework, with the first notes in circulation in 2020. In Germany, the Bundesbank's tender for 2012 awarded Oberthur Technologies 526 million 10-euro notes. It then won a Bundesbank tender to print part of the euro banknotes for 2013, after an earlier award about two years before that losing bidders had challenged without success.
n:Crane Currency: Crane Currency is a banknote printer based in Dalton, United States. A release from Curaçao says it is headquartered in Massachusetts, has plants in Malta and Sweden, and supplies more than 50 central banks. Seven central banks are tied to it. It prints for Curaçao and Sint Maarten (the new Caribbean guilder), Liberia, and Tanzania, where Crane Currency of Malta was one of two winners of a tender reported on 28 May 2024 to reprint the 10,000, 5,000, 2,000 and 1,000 shilling notes. It has supplied banknotes or related materials to Mexico, Guyana and Aruba. It has supplied banknote paper and security features to the US Treasury since 1879, though the customer there is the Treasury, not the Federal Reserve. In Liberia, Crane printed under two contracts totalling 15 billion Liberian dollars at a cost of US$15,331,689.20. A presidential investigation team alleged that Crane conspired with Central Bank of Liberia officials to print 18,151,000,000 Liberian dollars, more than contracted, and its report also named former governor Charles Sirleaf. Crane denied wrongdoing and kickbacks and said it had not been charged. This is an allegation and no court has found it proven.
n:Goznak: Goznak is the Russian state printer, based in Moscow. It printed Libyan dinars for the eastern central bank in Benghazi and Bayda, which is not internationally recognized. Russian customs data cited by Reuters showed 4.5 billion dinars shipped between February and June 2019. On 1 November 2019 Malta seized two containers of the notes, citing United Nations resolutions that recognize only the government in Tripoli.
n:Giesecke+Devrient: Giesecke+Devrient is a banknote printer based in Munich, Germany, tied to three central banks. In Germany, the Bundesbank's tender for 2012 awarded it 526 million 10-euro notes. In Kenya, the central bank revealed a five-year deal with it worth 14.2 billion shillings (US$109,422,740), reported on 21 August 2024. In Myanmar, it supplied raw materials, supplies and system components for printing kyat banknotes to the state-owned Security Print Works, and suspended all deliveries after the military crackdown, in a press release issued in 2021. The customer there is the state printer, not the central bank.
n:Nigeria Security Printing and Minting: The Nigeria Security Printing and Minting Company (NSPMC) is a printing firm in Nigeria, shown on the map at the country rather than at its office. It printed the redesigned 2022 naira notes for the Central Bank of Nigeria. The anti-corruption agency EFCC verified payments from the central bank to the company as part of its four-count prosecution of former central bank governor Godwin Emefiele, who is charged with unlawfully printing new notes. These are charges, not a conviction.
n:State Street: State Street is a financial firm based in Boston, United States. It is tied to the Federal Reserve System. Under agreements dated 11 May 2020, State Street Bank and Trust Company is custodian, meaning it holds the assets, and administrator for Corporate Credit Facilities LLC. That company is the New York Fed vehicle for the PMCCF and SMCCF.
n:BNY Mellon: BNY Mellon is a bank based in New York, United States, tied to one central bank. In May 2020 the New York Fed selected The Bank of New York Mellon as custodian, which holds assets, and administrator for TALF 2020, the Term Asset-Backed Securities Loan Facility.
n:World Bank Treasury RAMP: RAMP is the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory & Management Partnership, based in Washington, United States. It serves nearly 100 members and manages over US$25 billion for them. Five central banks are tied to it. On 16 April 2026 Kosovo's central bank signed a new RAMP membership agreement, under which part of its reserves will be managed by RAMP from 2026. Ecuador's central bank was welcomed as a new member, Armenia's rejoined, and staff of the central banks of Trinidad and Tobago and Guatemala are featured as member institutions. For those four, membership alone does not show that RAMP manages their money.

n:Office of the Auditor-General: The Office of the Auditor-General in Kenya audits the accounts of the Central Bank of Kenya, the country's central bank. Its report for the year ended 30 June 2025 was issued on 7 October 2025.
n:SizweNtsalubaGobodo Grant Thornton Inc: SizweNtsalubaGobodo Grant Thornton Inc. is an auditing firm in South Africa. It audited the accounts of the South African Reserve Bank, the country's central bank, for the year ended 31 March 2023. Its independent auditors' report is dated 12 June 2023.
n:Badan Pemeriksa Keuangan (BPK), Republ: Badan Pemeriksa Keuangan (BPK) is Indonesia's state audit body. It audits the accounts of Bank Indonesia, the country's central bank. Kontan reported on 25 June 2025 that Bank Indonesia again received an unqualified opinion (a clean audit result) from the BPK for 2024.
n:French Treasury: The French Treasury is a government body based in Paris, France. It is tied to 15 central banks, and ten of them are: the Central Bank of West African States (BCEAO) as it operates in Benin, Burkina Faso, Côte d'Ivoire, Guinea-Bissau, Mali, Niger, Senegal and Togo, and the Bank of Central African States (BEAC) in Cameroon and the Central African Republic. In each case the tie is a guarantee. France backs the currency the bank issues under a cooperation agreement. The West African CFA franc is fixed at 1 euro for 655.957 CFA francs, and France promises unconditional and unlimited convertibility, meaning it advances money to the central bank if its foreign exchange reserves run out. The Central African CFA franc has the same rate. The euro replaced the French franc as its anchor on 1 January 1999 with no change in the rate, and France commits euro funds if the region cannot pay for imports in foreign currency. These are cooperation arrangements, and the text reports no wrongdoing.
n:Government of Portugal: The Government of Portugal is based in Lisbon, Portugal. It is tied to one central bank, the Bank of Cape Verde. Portugal guarantees the currency that bank issues, the Cabo Verde escudo, under a cooperation agreement on exchange rates. The agreement, called the Acordo de Cooperação Cambial, was signed on 13 March 1998. The rate was set at 0.55 Cape Verde escudos per Portuguese escudo, and it became 110.265 Cape Verde escudos per euro. This is a currency arrangement between the two countries, and no wrongdoing is reported.
n:AKO Capital LLP: AKO Capital LLP is an investment firm in London. Nicolai Tangen, the incoming chief executive of the fund arm of Norges Bank, Norway's central bank, had a holding in it. In August 2020, after the Storting's finance committee raised conflict-of-interest concerns, the bank's board rewrote his terms: he would give up that holding and transfer it and its dividend rights to the charitable AKO Foundation, with no ownership interest in perpetuity. Supervisory Board chair Julie Brodtkorb said guidelines, regulations and laws had been breached in the appointment. Tangen took office on 1 September.
n:Argentine judiciary: The Argentine judiciary, the country's court system, features in a dispute over who controls the Central Bank of the Argentine Republic. In a page dated 30 January 2010, Argentina's central bank chief Martin Perez Redrado resigned amid a dispute with President Cristina Kirchner. An Argentine court had determined that Kirchner needed the approval of the full Congress to use the bank's reserves, and the reserves stayed frozen while lawmakers were expected to take the matter up in March.
n:Bank of Ceylon: Bank of Ceylon is a bank based in Colombo, Sri Lanka. An Anti-Corruption Commission report made public in February 2019 found the Maldives Monetary Authority, the Maldives' central bank, negligent over the embezzlement of 1.3 billion rufiyaa from Maldives Marketing and Public Relations Corporation. Its Financial Intelligence Unit, the office that examines suspicious money, was told in 2014 of a 59 million US dollar cheque from that company to a firm called SOF, did not investigate it properly, and never looked at SOF's large transactions through Bank of Maldives and Bank of Ceylon.
n:CLICO: CLICO is an insurer based in Port of Spain, Trinidad & Tobago. At the Commission of Enquiry into the collapse of CL Financial and the Hindu Credit Union, Queen's Counsel Peter Carter put it to former Central Bank governor Ewart Williams on 6 December 2012 that if the bank had intervened in 2006, over 10 billion Trinidad and Tobago dollars would not have been at risk. Williams said the bank saw warning signs at CLICO in 2006 but held off to avoid a run, and intervened in 2009. That was cross-examination, not a commission finding, so it is unproven.
n:Commission of Inquiry into the financi: This was a Gambian public inquiry, based in Banjul, into the finances of former president Yahya Jammeh, and it examined the Central Bank of The Gambia. The government's White Paper accepted its finding that between September 2015 and January 2017 General Sulayman Badjie, purportedly acting for Jammeh, instructed the Governor or his deputies to withdraw US dollars, and that the Governor handed cash to soldiers. The Commission held Badjie accountable for illegal withdrawals of 15,785,601 US dollars, 300,000 euros and 9,606,000 dalasis, and the government ordered the money recovered by forfeiting and selling his properties. It also records 28.5 million US dollars illegally granted in the bank's 3M Account in 2000 and 2001.
n:Direccion de Persecucion de la Corrupc: This is the Dominican Republic's office for prosecuting corruption in public administration, based in Santo Domingo. It took former central bank governor Jose Lois Malkun, former deputy governor Felix Calvo, former administrative director Cesar Apolinar Veloz and former legal counsel Manuel Rubio Cristoforis to court on charges including breach of trust and criminal association, over the disappearance of 18 promissory notes worth 10,663 million Dominican pesos said to have been handed fraudulently to former banker Manuel Arturo Pellerano. The charges are unproven. The central bank did not complain or join as a civil party; a Junta Monetaria resolution said its authorities were negotiating the notes' return.
n:Farmers Bank: Farmers Bank is a bank in Eswatini. In 2017 an evaluations team at the Central Bank of Eswatini recommended refusing it a commercial banking licence, and the application was turned down late that year. In May 2018 finance minister Martin Dlamini told the central bank the king had ordered an investigation into its reluctance to license it, and a conditional licence followed in September 2018 after a royal command from King Mswati III. The central bank revoked it on 5 October 2020 because the source of the seed capital was unexplained; commerce minister Manqoba Khumalo ruled that December that the bank should keep it, and the central bank reinstated it in January 2021. A 2022 Kroll report said outside parties had likely instructed the central bank to proceed, and that 89 million rand of seed capital went into silver bullion the central bank could not verify existed.
n:Hindu Credit Union: The Hindu Credit Union was a lender in Trinidad & Tobago whose collapse, with that of CL Financial, was examined by a commission of enquiry commissioned in November 2010 under sole commissioner Sir Anthony Colman. It found the Central Bank of Trinidad and Tobago's powers to regulate insurers 'fundamentally deficient', because of the narrow scope of the Insurance Act, and said the Inspector of financial institutions used the limited tools available but that Clico and CL Financial management largely ignored them. It blamed no named Central Bank official, and sat from March 2011 to May 2013.
n:Kisutu Resident Magistrate's Court: The Kisutu Resident Magistrate's Court sits in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. It sentenced businessmen Farijala Hussein and Rajabu Maranda to five years in prison, finding them guilty of offences related to financial impropriety, forgery and obtaining credit under false pretences, and ordered them to return the money they had taken. A report published on 27 May 2011 describes these as the first court cases heard after the 2008 Bank of Tanzania corruption scandal.
n:Manuel Arturo Pellerano: Manuel Arturo Pellerano is a former banker in the Dominican Republic. The country's office for prosecuting corruption in public administration took former central bank governor Jose Lois Malkun, former deputy governor Felix Calvo, former administrative director Cesar Apolinar Veloz and former legal counsel Manuel Rubio Cristoforis to court on charges including breach of trust and criminal association, over the disappearance of 18 promissory notes worth 10,663 million Dominican pesos said to have been handed fraudulently to Pellerano. The charges are unproven. The central bank did not complain or join as a civil party; a Junta Monetaria resolution said its authorities were negotiating the notes' return with him.
n:Ministerio Publico de Chile: The Ministerio Publico is Chile's public prosecution service, based in Santiago. In March 2022 someone posing as the chief financial officer of the US firm RVK emailed the Central Bank of Chile a false invoice for 205,000 US dollars from an address one letter different from the real one, and the bank paid. It complained to prosecutors on 20 May 2022 and opened an internal investigation, saying there was no indication any official took part deliberately. It dismissed the head of its accounting management department on 23 June 2022; he sued in December, calling the dismissal abusive and seeking 267 million pesos.
n:Nicolae Timofti: Nicolae Timofti was president of Moldova, based in Chisinau. Dorin Dragutanu resigned as governor of the National Bank of Moldova after criticism for failing to prevent about 1 billion US dollars disappearing from three Moldovan banks in 2014. He said he was resigning because of pressure from some politicians, and denied responsibility, saying he had repeatedly warned the authorities. Timofti and Prime Minister Valeriu Strelet had both said he should be removed.
n:Paetongtarn Shinawatra: Paetongtarn Shinawatra leads the Pheu Thai Party in Bangkok. She criticised the Bank of Thailand's independence, saying the law that keeps the bank separate from the government obstructs solving economic problems. The remarks drew a backlash, and Prime Minister Srettha Thavisin said he had no plans to remove Governor Sethaput Suthiwartnarueput or to amend the Bank of Thailand Act. A 2008 amendment to that Act makes removing the governor over policy disagreements very difficult.
n:RVK: RVK is a firm based in the United States. In March 2022 someone posing as its chief financial officer emailed the Central Bank of Chile a false invoice for 205,000 US dollars, from an address differing from the real one by a single letter, and asked for payment to a new account at another bank; the bank paid. The bank complained to the public prosecution service in May 2022 and dismissed the head of its accounting management department on 23 June 2022; he sued in December, calling the dismissal abusive and unfair and seeking 267 million pesos.
n:Seoul Central District Court: The Seoul Central District Court sits in Seoul, South Korea. A former Bank of Korea employee, moved in 2013 to the museum operations team and responsible for paying in the proceeds of the bank's publication sales, diverted about 56 million won in 14 transfers to a personal account and used a corporate card to buy about 12 million won of commemorative uncut banknote sheets. Judge Lee Heung-kwon convicted the employee of occupational breach of trust and embezzlement and imposed eight months in prison suspended for two years, noting the full amount had been repaid.
n:Supreme Court of Appeal of Bahrain: The Supreme Court of Appeal of Bahrain sits in Manama. It upheld a Court of First Instance ruling convicting the Central Bank of Iran, together with a number of Iranian banks, Future Bank and six Future Bank officials, as announced by attorney general Wael Bualai. Each convicted party, including the Central Bank of Iran, was fined one million Bahraini dinars; five Future Bank officials received ten-year prison sentences and the sixth five years. The court upheld confiscation of remittances put at 184 million US dollars, 967 million euros, 53 million dirhams and 235 billion Iranian rials.
n:Transitional government of Madagascar: Madagascar's transitional government, based in Antananarivo, dismissed central bank governor Frederic Rasamoely in February 2012. Bank employees staged a sit-in, saying the removal went against the bank's independence, and said the strike would continue while they challenged the new governor's appointment.
n:Wlodzimierz Czarzasty: Wlodzimierz Czarzasty is Marshal of the Sejm, Poland's lower house of parliament. In October 2026 the Sejm's Committee on Constitutional Responsibility adopted a report supporting the referral of National Bank of Poland president Adam Glapinski to the State Tribunal, and Czarzasty said the full chamber would vote in the second half of November 2026. The motion, begun in May 2024, accuses Glapinski of indirectly financing the budget deficit through asset purchases in 2020 and 2021 and of acting without proper authorisation from the Monetary Policy Council. Glapinski and the bank called the allegations baseless, and no vote had been held.
n:AKO Foundation: The AKO Foundation is a charity in the United Kingdom. In August 2020, after the Storting's finance committee raised conflict-of-interest concerns, Norges Bank's Executive Board rewrote the terms of its incoming investment chief, Nicolai Tangen: he would sell his holding in AKO Capital, transfer that holding and its dividend rights to the AKO Foundation with no ownership interest in AKO Capital in perpetuity, and hold his personal fund assets as bank deposits. Supervisory Board chair Julie Brodtkorb said his appointment had breached guidelines, regulations and laws. Tangen took office on 1 September.
n:Art-B: Art-B was a Polish company at the centre of a cheque-float scheme, in which money is drawn against cheques that have not yet cleared. Its owners fled in the summer of 1991, and arrests followed. Among those arrested was Grzegorz Wojtowicz, president of Narodowy Bank Polski, the country's central bank. He was charged with unintentionally causing bank losses of about 72 billion old zloty, and the court acquitted him. Prison sentences went to several employees of state banks.
n:Bank of Georgia: Bank of Georgia is a commercial bank in Tbilisi. At a briefing on 20 September 2023 the acting president of the National Bank of Georgia, Natia Turnava, confirmed she had single-handedly changed the procedure for carrying out sanctions regimes, adopting it on 19 September and making it effective the next day, and said she had told National Bank Council members in advance. Bank of Georgia and TBC Bank had frozen the accounts of Otar Partskhaladze; Turnava said they broke no law, because the amendment took effect the day she spoke. Vice-president Papuna Lezhava resigned.
n:Caixa Geral de Depositos: Caixa Geral de Depositos is a bank in Lisbon. In April 2019, after an EY audit of CGD's management, the Bank of Portugal's ethics committee examined a request by governor Carlos Costa to be excused from matters concerning CGD. Costa had sat on CGD's board from 2004 to 2006 and may have taken part in extended credit council meetings that approved operations which caused losses, while now heading the supervisor assessing former CGD directors. Vice-governor Elisa Ferreira did not recuse herself but reported a possible conflict over her husband's past role at La Seda. The committee's conclusions were not made public.
n:Constitutional Tribunal of Poland: The Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw decides whether Polish laws fit the constitution. The ruling coalition accused National Bank of Poland governor Adam Glapinski of breaking several laws and of failing to uphold the bank's political independence under the former Law and Justice government, and in March 2024 it asked the Sejm to bring him before the State Tribunal, which tries holders of high office. A ruling of 12 January 2024 had set the bar at a three-fifths majority, and the coalition held 241 of 460 seats against a threshold of 276. On 20 August 2024 a five-judge panel including chief justice Julia Przylebska ruled the legislation allowing him to be brought before the constitutional accountability committee unconstitutional.
n:District Prosecutor's Office in Warsaw: The District Prosecutor's Office in Warsaw is the state prosecution service for the Polish capital. It is investigating how information classified as secret got out of the closed part of the National Bank of Poland's Monetary Policy Council meeting of 8 September 2023, after a complaint by one of the Council's members. A court had earlier overturned a decision refusing to open the investigation. On 12 June 2025 prosecutors secured documents at the bank's head office, after the bank had twice refused to hand them over.
n:Financial Action Task Force: The Financial Action Task Force, based in Paris, sets the international standards countries are judged against on money laundering, and keeps a grey list of those whose enforcement it finds wanting. It added Mongolia to that list over money-laundering enforcement, and Mongolian lawmakers accepted the resignation of central bank governor Nadmid Bayartsaikhan on 21 November 2019, after he resigned over the listing. Parliament appointed Byadran Lkhagvasuren the next day.
n:Inter-American Development Bank: The Inter-American Development Bank, based in Washington, D.C., lends for development in Latin America and the Caribbean. Karnit Flug, who later ran Israel's central bank, worked there as a senior research economist from 1994 to 1996. She had joined the International Monetary Fund as an economist in 1984 and the Bank of Israel's Research Department in 1988. She became Deputy Governor of the Bank of Israel in July 2011 and was appointed Governor on 13 November 2013.
n:Kroll: Kroll is a corporate investigations firm in the United States, commissioned by the Central Bank of Eswatini. In 2017 the bank's evaluations team recommended refusing Farmers Bank a commercial banking licence, warning it would tarnish the integrity of the bank's licensing policy, and the application was rejected; a conditional licence followed in September 2018 after a royal command from King Mswati III. Governor Majozi Sithole said he was given a royal command to attend a meeting about the bank on 14 July 2017, and in May 2018 finance minister Martin Dlamini said the king had ordered an investigation into the bank's reluctance to license it. The central bank revoked the licence on 5 October 2020 over the unexplained source of the seed capital; commerce minister Manqoba Khumalo ruled in December 2020 that it should be kept, and the bank reinstated it in January 2021 while objecting to procedural improprieties. Kroll's 2022 report said third parties outside the bank had likely intervened and instructed it to proceed, and that 89 million rand of seed capital had gone from 2019 into silver bullion the bank could not verify existed.
n:Manuel Chang: Manuel Chang, of Mozambique, is named in the hidden debts case, over more than two billion US dollars of loans from Credit Suisse and VTB of Russia to the companies Proindicus, Ematum and MAM.
